(Surat al-Nur is Medinan, and it contains sixty-four verses, or sixty-two according to some counts.)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿A surah﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., this is a surah. It is pointed to (with "this") even though it has not been mentioned before, because by virtue of its being in the status of honour and remembrance it is treated as present and witnessed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have sent it down﴾, together with what is conjoined to it, are attributes of it that emphasise what the indefiniteness (of "surah") conveys of grandeur in respect of its essence, by grandeur in respect of its attributes. As for taking it as the subject of an omitted predicate, so that the sense would be "among what We have revealed to you is a surah which We have sent down," this is rejected, because the context calls for explaining the status of the noble surah, not for stating that among the things revealed to the Prophet ﷺ there is a surah with such-and-such a status; and understanding it as referring to the noble surah by the aid of context suggests that other noble surahs do not possess those attributes. It has also been read in the accusative, by supposing a verb that is explained by ﴿We have sent it down﴾; in that case it has no place in the grammatical structure, or (it is supposed) as "recite" or the like, or "take it" (duna-ka) according to those who permit omitting the particle of incitement; then the place of ﴿We have sent it down﴾ is accusative by way of being a descriptive clause.

﴿And We have made it obligatory﴾, i.e., or We have made obligatory the rulings contained in it with a definitive obligation. In this there is an indication of the utmost emphasis on its obligatoriness that is not hidden. It has also been read as "farradnaha" with the doubled letter, to stress the obligation, or because of the multiplicity of obligations, or because of the great number of those upon whom it was made obligatory from the earlier and later generations.

﴿And in it We have sent down﴾, i.e., within its contents, ﴿clear signs﴾. If by them is meant the verses to which the obligatory rulings are attached, which is the more apparent reading, then their being in the surah is evident; and the meaning of their being "clear" is the clarity of their indications of their rulings, not of their meanings in an absolute sense, for they are like all other verses in this respect. The repetition of "We have sent down" along with the fact that sending down the surah entails sending down its verses serves to display complete care for its matter. If by them is meant all the verses, then the expression "in it" is taken in regard to the whole comprising each of its parts. The repetition of "We have sent down", even though all the verses are the surah itself and their sending down is the same as its sending down, is due to the surah being distinguished by an attractive title which calls for singling out its sending down for mention, to make known its importance and to elevate its station, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We saved them from a severe punishment﴾ after His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us﴾.

﴿So that you may remember﴾, with one of the two taa' elided; it has also been read with the second taa' assimilated into the dhal, i.e., "so that you may remember them" and thus know by their requirement at the occurrence of events which call for the implementation of their rulings. In this there is an indication that it is proper for them to be in remembrance on their part, such that whenever need arises for them they bring them to mind.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 2:

﴿The adulterer and the adulteress﴾ is the beginning of the detailing of what was mentioned of the clear signs and the explanation of their rulings. (p-156) Al-zaniyah (the adulteress) is the woman who submits to fornication and enables it, as the form of the word indicates, not one who is forcibly violated. Her being placed before the adulterer (al-zani) is because she is the origin of the act, since the inciting motive in her is stronger, and had she not enabled him, it would not have occurred. Both are in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾. The fa' (then) is for the subject containing the meaning of a conditional, since the alif-lam is in the sense of a relative pronoun, and the estimate is: "the woman who committed fornication and the man who committed fornication," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those two of you who commit it, harm them﴾. It has been said: the predicate is omitted, meaning: "in what We have sent down" or "in what We have enjoined, the adulteress and the adulterer," that is, their ruling. His saying, exalted is He, "flog..." etc., is an explanation of that ruling. This was general concerning the married and others, and it was abrogated concerning the married definitively. What suffices us in identifying the abrogating text is the certainty that the Prophet ﷺ stoned Ma'iz or others, so this falls under the category of the abrogation of the Book by the well-known Sunnah. In al-Idah it is stated: stoning is a ruling established by the well-known Sunnah agreed upon, so an addition to the Book by it is permissible. It is reported from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "I flogged her by the Book of Allah and I stoned her by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." It has also been said: it was abrogated by a verse whose recitation was abrogated, namely: "the old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as a punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise." This is rejected by what is reported from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿And let not compassion for them seize you﴾: it was also read with a fatha on the hamza and with a long vowel, on the pattern fa'alah, meaning mercy and tenderness.

﴿in the religion of Allah﴾: in obedience to Him and in establishing His prescribed punishment, lest you suspend it or be lenient regarding it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ has said: ﴿If Fatimah daughter of Muhammad had stolen, I would have cut off her hand.﴾

﴿if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾: this is in the manner of stirring up and inciting, for belief in these two requires earnestness in His obedience, exalted is He, and striving in carrying out His rulings. The mention of the Last Day is to remind of the punishment in it, in contrast to leniency and suspension.

﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾: that is, let them be present for it as an increase in deterrence, for public exposure may deter more than punishment itself. A ṭā'ifah (group) is a company that may be encircling something of the circumambulation, and its least number is three, as reported from Qatadah; and from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: four to forty; and from al-Hasan: ten. What is intended is a gathering by which public exposure and deterrence are achieved.

The ruling that "the fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or a polytheist, and the fornicatress is not married except by a fornicator or a polytheist" is founded upon what is usual and customary, and it was revealed to deter the believers from them. Some of the weaker among the emigrants (muhajirun) desired to marry certain prostitutes of the polytheists who were in Medina, so they asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission in this matter. He turned them away by explaining that it is among the deeds of fornicators and the characteristics of polytheists. It is as if it were said: the fornicator desires only to marry one of these two, and the fornicatress is desired in marriage only by one of these two; so do not hover around them, lest you be enrolled in their line or bear their mark. The mention of the first clause, although the point of deterrence lies in the second, is either by way of allusion, restricting their desire to these women since they asked to marry them, or to emphasize the connection between the two sides, as an intensification of the deterrence and repulsion. In the second clause, the polytheist woman is not mentioned, to draw attention to the fact that the basis of the prohibition and repulsion is fornication, not mere association (shirk). He mentioned her in the first clause to amplify the repulsion from the fornicatress by placing her in the same line as the polytheist woman.

"And that was forbidden" (﴿وَحُرِّمَ ذَلِكَ﴾), that is, marrying fornicators, "upon the believers" (﴿عَلى المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾), because it contains resemblance to the wicked, exposure to suspicion, causing evil talk, impugning lineage, disruption of the affairs of livelihood, and other corruptions that scarcely befit anyone of the base and lowly, let alone the believers. For this reason, the disapproval (tanzih) is expressed by the term prohibition (tahrim), as an intensification of the deterrence. It has also been said that the negation carries the meaning of a prohibition, and it has been read that way. The prohibition is in its literal sense, and the ruling is either specific to the occasion of revelation, or abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And marry off the single among you...﴾, for it encompasses those who commit fornication. This is supported by what is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about this and said: "Its beginning is fornication and its end is marriage, and the unlawful does not make the lawful unlawful." As for what has been said, that the meaning of marriage here is intercourse, it is clearly invalid.

﴿Those who accuse chaste women﴾ is an explanation of the ruling concerning chaste women when they are accused of illicit intercourse, following the explanation of the ruling concerning adulterers. What is required for *ihsan* (chastity or protected status, *al-ihsan*) here, together with its literal meaning, which is abstention from illicit intercourse, is freedom, puberty and Islam. The expression of uttering what they said about them by *ramy* (throwing), which indicates the hardness of the instrument and the pain inflicted on the one thrown at, and its distance from the one who throws, is a notice of the severity of its effect upon them and of its being "stoning in the unseen." What is meant by it is accusing them of illicit intercourse and nothing else. The explicit mention of it is omitted because it is sufficient to mention them immediately after the adulterers and to describe them with *ihsan*, which by its literal meaning indicates their purity from illicit intercourse specifically, since that is equivalent to an explicit statement that their accusation is necessarily of that kind. There is no need, in this regard, to cite the consideration of four witnesses, nor the non-obligation of the *hadd* (prescribed punishment) for accusing with something other than illicit intercourse, since that would entail the burden of explaining that the revelation of this verse came after His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then bring four witnesses against them﴾, nor would it avoid the fallacy of begging the question. As if it were said: "Those who accuse the chaste, the pure, free of what they were accused of, namely illicit intercourse."

﴿Then do not bring four witnesses﴾ who testify against them concerning what they accused them of. In the word "then" (*thumma*) there is an indication that bringing the witnesses may be delayed, just as in the word "not" (*lam*) there is an indication of establishing the inability to bring them and confirming it. Except that the gathering of the witnesses is necessary at the time of giving testimony, contrary to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, for he permitted delay between the testimonies, just as between the throwing (accusation) and the testimony. It is also permissible that one of them be the husband of the accused woman, contrary to him as well. It has been recited: "bi-arba'ati shuhada'" (with four witnesses).

﴿Then flog them eighty lashes﴾ because their lying and fabrication are made manifest by their inability to bring witnesses, in accordance with His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when they have not brought the witnesses, then those are the liars in the sight of Allah﴾. The accusative of "eighty" is like the accusative of verbal nouns (*masadir*), and the accusative of "lashes" (*jaldah*) is by way of specification (*tamyiz*). The specification of their accusation with this ruling, although the ruling for accusing married (*muhsinin*) men is likewise, is due to the particular occasion and the prevalence of accusation concerning them.

﴿And do not accept testimony from them﴾ is coordinated with "flog" and enters into its ruling as a completion of it, because it contains the sense of deterrence, since it is painful to the heart just as flogging is painful to the body. He has harmed the accused with his tongue, so he is punished by the forfeiture of his benefits as a fitting recompense. The preposition in "for them" (*lahum*) is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from "testimony," placed before it because it is indefinite; had it been placed after it, it would have been an adjective of it. Its benefit is the restriction of the rejection to their testimony arising from their qualification that was established for them at the time of accusation. This is the secret of the acceptance of the testimony of the disbelieving person who has been punished by *hadd* for slander after repentance and Islam, because it does not arise from his previous qualification but from a qualification that came into being for him after his Islam, so the rejection does not cover it. Reflect on this, and set aside what has been said, that Muslims do not care about the causes of disbelievers, so the shame and disgrace that befall the one accused by a disbeliever are not the same as those that befall one accused by a Muslim. For that, without the consideration mentioned, is a rationale set against the explicit text, and its unsoundness is not hidden. So the meaning is: do not accept from them any testimony of testimonies, while it is being (*hasilatan*) theirs at the time of accusation, ﴿ever﴾, that is, for the duration of their lives, even if they repent and reform, in accordance with what you have learned, that it is a completion of the *hadd*. As if it were said: flog them and reject their testimony; that is, combine for them the flogging and the rejection, and it remains as its origin.

﴿And those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ is a resumed statement confirming what precedes it and clarifying the wretchedness of their state in the sight of Allah, mighty and majestic. The sense of distance in the demonstrative (*ism al-isharah*) is to indicate the remoteness of their rank in evil and corruption. That is: those are the ones judged as defiantly disobedient, who have departed from obedience and transgressed the limits, the complete ones in it, as if they alone deserve the application of the name "defiantly disobedient" (*fasiq*) to them, and not others among the transgressors.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 5:

As for His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Except those who repent﴾, it is an exception from "the defiantly disobedient" (al-fasiqun), as the subsequent reasoning (ta'lil) indicates. The place of the excepted item (al-mustathna) is in the accusative (nasb), because it is from an affirmative (mujab) statement.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿after that﴾, it is to magnify the matter from which they repent, i.e., after they committed that great and terrible sin. ﴿And made amends﴾, i.e., they reformed their deeds, among which is making good what they had neglected by compensation and making up for it, and among this is surrendering themselves to the prescribed punishment (hadd) and seeking the pardon of the one who was slandered.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for what the exception implies of pardon from being held accountable for the consequence of defiant disobedience, as if it were said: Then Allah, the Exalted, will not hold them accountable for what they neglected, nor will He count them among the defiantly disobedient, because He, the Exalted, is abundant in forgiveness and mercy.

Furthermore, al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, made the exception conditional upon the prohibition (al-nahy). Accordingly, the place of the excepted item is then the genitive (jarr) by way of substitution (badal) from the pronoun in "for them." He took "abadan" (forever) to be an expression for the period during which he remains a slanderer, so it ends with repentance, and his testimony is then accepted after it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 6:

﴿And those who accuse their wives﴾ is a statement of the ruling concerning those who accuse their own wives specifically, after the statement of the ruling concerning those who accuse other women. But this does not mean that it specifies (takhsis) the chaste women (al-muhsanat) to mean strangers (al-ajnabiyyat), for that would leave the preceding verse speculative (zanniyyah) and so the hadd punishment would not be established by it. Among the conditions of takhsis is that the specifying evidence not be later in revelation (mutarakhi al-nuzul). Rather, this verse is an abrogation (naskh, the lifting of a earlier ruling by a later one) of the general scope of the preceding verse, since its revelation came later, as will come. Thus the preceding verse remains definitive in meaning (qat'iyyat al-dalalah) regarding what remains after the abrogation, as has been explained in its proper place, that the evidence of abrogation is not based on a rationale.

﴿And they have no witnesses﴾ who testify to the adultery with which they accused them. It is also read with the verb in the feminine form.

﴿except themselves﴾ is a substitute for "witnesses," or an attribute of it, on the basis that "illa" here means "ghayr" (other than). They are counted among the witnesses, as a notice from the outset that their statement is not wholly disregarded and that it is placed within the category of testimony in general. Because of this, the attribution of testimony to them in the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿So the testimony of one of them﴾, that is, the testimony of each one of them, becomes more fitting. Here "fashahadatu" is the subject (mubtada'), and His words ﴿four testimonies﴾ are its predicate (khabar). That is, their prescribed testimony is four testimonies. ﴿by Allah﴾ is related to "shahadat" because it is closest to it, and it is said that it is related to "shahadah" because it precedes it. It is also read as "arba'a shahadat" in the accusative, as a verbal noun (masdar), with the governing element being "fashahadatu." On this reading, it is either the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "so what is obligatory is the testimony of one of them," or the subject of an omitted predicate, meaning: "so the testimony of one of them is obligatory."

﴿Indeed he is among the truthful﴾ means: in what he has accused her of regarding adultery. Its original form is "'ala annahu" and so on, where the preposition is omitted, "inna" is made with a kasra, and the governing element is suspended from it for emphasis.

(p-159) ﴿And the fifth﴾: that is, the fifth testimony, in addition to the preceding four. That is, it makes their number five by being joined to them, and it is set apart from them even though it too is a testimony, because it stands on its own in meaning and is emphatic in conveying what testimony aims at, namely establishing the report and manifesting truthfulness. Its predicate (khabar) is ﴿that the curse of Allah be upon him if he is among the liars﴾, concerning what he attributed to her of fornication. So when the husband performs the li'an (mutual imprecation, lu'an), the wife is detained until she confesses, whereupon she is stoned, or she performs the li'an in turn.

**Qur'an 24:8:** "And it shall avert from her the punishment (al-'adhab)…"

That is, the worldly punishment, which is confinement (al-habs) that is limited (al-mughayya) according to one of the two opinions by stoning (al-rajm), which is the most severe of punishments, "that she testify four testimonies by Allah that he (ﷺ)…" — rather, that he (i.e., the husband) "is surely among the liars" — that is, in what he has accused her of, namely adultery (al-zina).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 9:

﴿And the fifth﴾ in the accusative (naṣb), [as a substitute] for the four testimonies, [saying] ﴿that the wrath of Allah be upon her if he is among the truthful﴾, i.e., the husband, ﴿among the truthful﴾, meaning: in what he has accused her of regarding adultery. It has also been read as "wal-khāmisatu" in the nominative (rafʿ), as a subject (ibtidāʾ), and it has been read as "an" with the light form (takhfīf) in both places, with "al-laʿnah" and "al-ghaḍab" in the nominative. It has also been read as "an ghaḍiba Allāh." The specification of the wrath to the woman's side is for emphasis against her, since she is the source of immorality, and because women frequently use the curse (al-laʿn), so they may become bold in uttering it, its impact having fallen from their hearts, unlike His exalted wrath. It is related that when the verse of slander (qadhf) was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it on the pulpit, and ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdiyy al-Anṣārī (may Allah be pleased with him) stood up and said: "May Allah make me your ransom! If a man finds another man with his wife and reports it, he is flogged eighty lashes, his testimony is rejected, and he is declared a wrongdoer (fāsiq). And if he strikes him with a sword, he is killed. And if he remains silent, he remains silent in rage. And until he brings four witnesses, the man has already fulfilled his need and departed. O Allah, open [the matter]!" He went out, and Hilāl ibn Umayya, or ʿUwaymir, met him and said: "What is behind you?" He said: "Evil. I found a man with my wife Khawla, who is the daughter of ʿĀṣim, the partner of Ibn Saḥmāʾ." Hilāl said: "By Allah, this is my question. How quickly you have been tested by it!" So the two returned and informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he spoke to Khawla, but she denied it. Then the verse was revealed, and he had them perform the mutual curse (liʿān) between them.

The separation (furqa) that occurs through li'ān is, according to Abu Hanifa and Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on them both), in the status of an irrevocable single divorce (taṭlīqa bāʾina), and its ruling is not made permanent; so if the man retracts his accusation of himself after that and is subjected to the prescribed punishment (ḥadd), it is permissible for him to marry her. According to Abu Yusuf, Zufar, al-Hasan ibn Ziyad, and al-Shafiʿi (may Allah have mercy on them all): it is a separation without divorce, which entails a permanent prohibition (taḥrīm mu'abbad), such that the two may never reunite after that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 10:

﴿And were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy, and that Allah is Oft-Relenting (tawwab), All-Wise (hakim)...﴾ This is a shift (iltifat) to address the accusers and the accused together, by way of prevalence (taghlib), so that the occasion of bestowing favour is given its due. The answer to "law la" (lawla, "had it not been for") is omitted, both to magnify it and to signal that expression falls short of encompassing it. It is as if it were said: "And had it not been for His grace upon you, His mercy, and that He is exceedingly accepting of repentance and All-Wise in all His acts and rulings, among which is what He prescribed for you of the ruling of li'an (mutual imprecation), what happened would have been beyond the reach of expression." Among its aspects: had He not prescribed that for them, the husband would have been subject to the punishment for slander (hadd al-qadhf), although the apparent truth is that he is sincere, since he knows his wife's condition best and he would not falsely accuse her, given that they share the disgrace. And after He prescribed it for them, had He made his testimonies (p-160) necessitate the punishment for adultery upon her, the consideration for her would have been lost; and had He made her testimonies necessitate the punishment for slander upon him, the consideration for him would have been lost. There is no doubt that all of this would depart from the courses of wisdom, grace and mercy. So He made the testimony of each of them, while being certain that one of them is definitely lying, a means of averting the worldly calamity directed at them. The liar among them has been tested, within the course of his testimonies, with a punishment greater and more complete than what it averted from him. In this are the decisions of profound wisdoms and the effects of grace and mercy that are not hidden. As for the truthful one, it is evident. As for the liar, it is His granting him respite, covering him in this world, averting the punishment from him, and offering him repentance, as is indicated by the mention of the title "Oft-Relenting" (tawwab). Glory be to Him, how great is His station, how vast His mercy, and how subtle His wisdom.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 11:

﴿Indeed, those who brought the slander﴾ means with the most eloquent form of lying and fabrication. It is also said that al-ifk (slander) is the most outrageous falsehood (buhtan), which takes you by surprise before you perceive it. Its root is al-ifk, which means "turning," because it is turned away from its true face and course. What is meant by it is that with which the truthful one (al-Siddiqah), Umm al-Mu'minin, may Allah be pleased with her, was slandered. The wording "brought" (ji'u) indicates that they fabricated it of their own accord, without it having any basis. This is because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, whenever he intended a journey, would draw lots among his wives, and whichever one's lot came out, he would take her with him. ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "He drew lots among us in a campaign he undertook. It is said it was the campaign of Banu al-Mustaliq. My lot came out, so I went out with him ﷺ after the revelation of the verse of hijab (veiling). I was carried in a howdah (litter), and we journeyed on. When we returned and drew near Madinah, we halted at a station. Then the call to depart was made. I got up and walked until I had passed the army. When I had finished my need, I came back to my riding-place and touched my chest, and behold, my necklace of Zafar onyx had broken, so I went back and searched for it, and my searching for it delayed me. Meanwhile, the men who used to prepare my riding-animal came, lifted my howdah and placed it on my camel, thinking I was inside it, because of my lightness. They did not notice the lightness of the howdah, and they set off with the camel. I found my necklace after the army had moved on, and I came to their campsite and there was no one there, no caller and no answerer. So I headed to my place, thinking that they would miss me and return to look for me. While I was sitting in my place, my eyes overcame me and I slept. Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal al-Sulami was behind the army, and when he saw me he recognized me, and I woke up at his saying 'Inna lillah' (istirja'). I covered my face with my jilbab. By Allah, we did not exchange a word, and I heard from him no word other than his istirja'. He dismounted and made his mount kneel, and he stepped on its forelegs, and I got up to it and rode it, and he set off leading the mount with me, until we reached the army at the height of midday while they were resting. The people missed me when they halted, and the folk were in an uproar over my absence. While the people were in that state, I appeared before them, and the people immersed themselves in discussing my affair, and those who were destroyed were destroyed."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿a band of you﴾ is the predicate of "inna" (indeed), meaning a group, which is between ten and forty, and likewise 'isaba (a band). They were ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy, Zayd ibn Rifa'a, Hassan ibn Thabit, Mistah ibn Uthatha, Hamnah bint Jahsh, and whoever assisted them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not consider it bad for you﴾ is a resumptive statement addressed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Abu Bakr, ʿĀʾisha and Safwan, may Allah be pleased with them all, as consolation for them from the outset of the matter. The pronoun refers to the slander.

﴿Rather, it is good for you﴾, since by it you earn great reward, your nobility before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, becomes manifest through the sending down of eighteen verses concerning the purity of your reputation, the magnifying of your standing, the strict warning concerning whoever spoke about you, and the praise of whoever thought well of you.

﴿For every man (p-161) of them﴾, that is, of those band, ﴿is what he earned of sin﴾, in proportion to what he immersed himself in. ﴿And he who took upon himself the greater part thereof﴾, that is, its largest share. It is also read with a dammah on the kaf (kibrahu), which is a dialect form of the same word.

﴿of them﴾, of the band, is ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy, for he initiated it and spread it among the people out of enmity toward the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It is also said that it was he, together with Hassan and Mistah, for they supported him by openly spreading it. The singular relative pronoun in that case is considered in terms of a group, a party, or the like.

﴿For him is a great punishment﴾, that is, in the Hereafter, or in this world also, for they were flogged, their testimony was rejected, Ibn Ubayy became expelled and testified against for hypocrisy, Hassan became blind and paralyzed in both hands, and Mistah became blind. In the expression of him by "the one who" (alladhi), the repetition of the predication, the indefiniteness of "punishment," and describing it as great, there is an amplification of the gravity of the matter that is not hidden.

This is an exposition of a verse, so I've translated the commentary as written, with the Qur'anic quotations rendered in plain English inside ﴿ ﴾.

﴿Why, when you heard it,﴾ is a *talwin* (shift of mode of address), a turning away of the address from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his household to those who were spreading the slander, by way of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), in order to intensify the reproach contained in *lawla al-tahdidiyya* (the "why not" particle that urges and rebukes). Then it turns from this to the third person in His words, exalted is He: ﴿the believing men and the believing women thought well of their own kind﴾, to emphasise the reproach and censure. However, this is not a turning away from them and a recounting of their offences to others in the manner of a warning, but rather a means of describing them with what necessitates doing what was urged, what strongly demands it, and what powerfully restrains them from its opposite. For the fact that the attribute of faith is among the things that moves them to think well and restrains them from harming it "by themselves", that is, by members of their own kind who stand in the position of themselves, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then you are those who kill yourselves﴾ and His words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not defame one another﴾, is beyond doubt. Their failure to act on what that attribute requires is therefore more abominable and more shameful, and the reproach for it is more fitting, along with what it contains of a means to state explicitly the reproach of the women who were spreading the slander.

Then, if by faith is meant true faith, its requirement for what has been mentioned is clear, and the reproach is specific to the believers. If, however, it is faith in its general sense, which includes what the hypocrites also outwardly display, then its requirement applies to them too, because they were careful to avoid showing what contradicts their claim. In that case the reproach is directed at all of them.

The placement of the adverbial phrase between *lawla* and its verb (*idh*, "when") serves to restrict the urging to the very first moment of their hearing it, and it confines the reproach to delaying the performance of what was urged, after that moment, and to hesitating about it. This is to convey that not performing it at all is at the extreme of ugliness and shamefulness. That is: it was obligatory that the believing men and believing women, at the first moment they heard it from the one who invented it, whether directly or through an intermediary, should think well of their own kind among the ordinary believers, without faltering or hesitation.

﴿And they said﴾ at that moment, ﴿This is a manifest lie﴾, that is, it is clear and evident that it is a lie. How much more so concerning the truthful one (*al-Siddiqa*), the daughter of the truthful one (*al-Siddiq*), the Mother of the Believers, the honoured wife of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 13:

﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses for it?﴾ This is either part of the speech that is being urged upon them (al-qawl al-muhadhdhad 'alayhi), introduced to incite the listeners to hold the slanderers accountable and to refute them, following the refutation of what they heard from them, by their saying: ﴿This is a manifest lie.﴾ It also rebukes them for not doing so. That is: Why did the slanderers not bring four witnesses who would testify to what they said?

﴿So when they do not bring the witnesses﴾ — the phrase is "bi-al-shuhada'" (with the witnesses) rather than "shuhada'" alone, for the sake of emphasizing the confirmation. ﴿Then those﴾ — the demonstrative refers to the slanderers, and the sense of distance in it indicates their extreme corruption and how far their station is from goodness. That is: those corrupters ﴿with Allah﴾, meaning in His judgment and His law, which is founded upon clear and perfectly sound proofs.

﴿They are the liars﴾ — those who are complete in lying, the lie being attested against them by that (non-production of witnesses), and who alone deserve to have the name applied to them to the exclusion of others. For this reason, the prescribed punishment (al-hadd) is specifically ordained upon them. Alternatively, this is an independent statement presented from Him, exalted is He, to argue against their lying, by the fact that what they said is a claim that the evidence does not support at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 14:

﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you﴾ is an address to all the listeners and those who spread (the report). ﴿And His mercy in this world﴾ is among the various kinds of blessings, of which one is the granting of respite for repentance. ﴿And the Hereafter﴾ is among the favours, of which one is pardon after repentance. ﴿Would have touched you﴾ immediately ﴿for that which you plunged into﴾ because of what you engaged in of the tale of the lie (ifk). The vagueness (al-ibham) serves to magnify its gravity and to express disgust at mentioning it. It is said: afada fi al-hadith, khada, indafa'a, and hadaba, all with the same meaning.

﴿a great punishment﴾, before which rebuke and flogging are deemed insignificant.

**﴿When you received it with your tongues﴾**: with the deletion of one of the two tāʾs, this is a temporal clause (ẓarf) governing the touching (al-massa): that is, that great punishment would have touched you at the time you received it from its inventors.

**﴿with your tongues﴾**: al-talaqqī, al-talaqquf and al-talaqqun (receiving, snatching up, and learning/taking in) are closely related meanings, except that the first carries the sense of meeting or facing something, the second the sense of snatching and seizing quickly, and the third the sense of skill and dexterity. It has been read as "tatalaqqawnahu" according to the original form; as "tulqūnahu" from liqiya (to meet); as "tilqūnahu" with the vowel of the present-tense prefix kasrah; as "tulqūnahu" from people casting (ilqāʾ) upon one another; as "talqawnahu" and "ta'lqūnahu" from al-walq and al-alq, which means lying; and as "tuthaqqifūnahu" from thaqafтu, meaning that when I seek something and find it; and "tuthaqqifūnahu," meaning "you make it wearisome" (tut'ibūnahu).

**﴿and you say with your mouths what you have no knowledge of﴾**: that is, you utter a statement confined to the mouths, without it having any reality (miṣdāq) or origin in the hearts, since it is not an expression of knowledge of it in your hearts, like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾.

**﴿and you reckon it to be trivial﴾**: easy, having no consequence, or having no great penalty.

**﴿while it is, in the sight of Allah﴾**: and the state is that it is with Him, mighty and majestic, **﴿great﴾**, its weight in sin and in drawing down punishment being beyond measure.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 16:

﴿Why, when you heard it﴾ from those who invented it and those who supported them, ﴿did you not say﴾, in denial of them and in amazement at what they had committed, ﴿It is not for us to speak of this﴾, meaning it is not possible for us, and nothing of this kind comes from us in any way. Its sense is the negation of the existence of speaking about it, not the negation of its existence in a sound, upright and suitable manner. This refers to what they heard. The placement of the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) between *lawlā* and *qultum* is because the urging (taḥḍīḍ, exhortation and reproach) is restricted to the first moment of hearing, and the rebuke and blame are confined to delaying the said statement beyond that moment. This indicates that the statement is one that could occur and therefore needs urging to abandon it. As for abandoning the statement altogether in matters whose occurrence is not imagined, so that one would be urged to do it and blamed for not doing it, this is not the case. On this basis, what has been said should be interpreted as follows: the meaning is that it was obligatory upon them to refrain from speaking of the slander at the very first moment they heard it. Since mentioning the time was more important, it had to be placed first.

As for what has been said, that the circumstances (ẓurūf) of things are treated as the things themselves because they occur within them and are inseparable from them, and therefore greater latitude is allowed in them than in other things, this is a general rule that is sometimes applied where the circumstance is placed in the position of what it contains, by making it an explicit object of a stated verb, as in the words of Him, exalted is He: ﴿And remember when He made you successors﴾, or by making it an implied object, as in the general case of accusative circumstances where *udhkurū* (remember) is understood. Here, however, there is no need for any of this at all, because it has been established that the basis of the placement is what makes the urging directed toward it necessary, and this is realized in all the related elements of the verb, as in the words of Him, exalted is He: ﴿Then why, if you are not to be held to account, do you not return it [the soul]?﴾

﴿Glory be to You﴾ is an expression of amazement at the one who utters it. Its original use is to be said upon witnessing something wondrous among the works of God, exalted is He, as a declaration of His transcendence, on the grounds that such a thing is difficult to produce. Then its usage became widespread until it was used for anything that causes amazement. Alternatively, it is a declaration of God's transcendence, exalted is He, above His Prophet's wife being unchaste, since her unchastity would repel people from him and undermine the purpose of marriage. Thus it serves as a confirmation of what precedes it and a preparation for His words, exalted is He: ﴿This is a great slander﴾, because of the greatness of what is being slandered and the impossibility of its being true. The lowliness or greatness of sins is determined by reference to what they relate to.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 17:

﴿Allah admonishes you﴾, i.e., advises you, ﴿never to return to the like of it﴾, i.e., out of aversion to returning to it, or He restrains you from returning to it, or [the construction is] "in returning to it," from the saying "I admonished him concerning such-and-such, so he abandoned it."

﴿Ever﴾, i.e., for the duration of your lives, ﴿if you are believers﴾. For faith is a restraint against it without doubt, and in this there is incitement and reproach.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 18:

﴿And Allah makes the signs clear for you﴾, the signs indicating the sacred laws (shara'i') and the excellent courtesies (mahasin al-adab), their indication being clear and manifest, so that you may take heed and be disciplined by them. That is: He sends them down in this manner, i.e., they are constructed and their indication of their meanings is apparent and manifest, not that He makes them clear after they were not so. This is like their saying: "Glory be to Him who made the gnat small and made the elephant large," i.e., He created the two of them small and large. And from it is your saying: "Narrow the mouth of the well, and widen its bottom." And the placing of the Divine Name in the position of a pronoun is a matter of clarification (shan al-bayan).

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of the states of all His creatures, the great and the minute.

﴿All-Wise﴾ in all His arrangements and actions. Therefore, how could what has been said about the honour of the one whom He chose for His messages and sent to all of mankind, to guide them to the truth, purify them and cleanse them thoroughly, be true? And the placing of the Divine Name here serves to emphasize the independence of the concluding parenthetical objection (al-i'tiradh al-tadhyili) and to indicate that the cause of divinity is knowledge and wisdom.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 19:

﴿Indeed, those who love﴾ i.e., desire and intend ﴿that indecency should spread﴾ i.e., that the extremely ugly conduct should become widespread, namely slander and the accusation of fornication, or fornication itself. The meaning of its "spreading" is the spreading of its report; i.e., they love its spread and at the same time strive for its dissemination. The matter was not stated explicitly, being sufficient with the mention of love, for it necessarily entails it.

﴿among those who believe﴾ is connected to "spread" (tusheee'a), i.e., that it spreads among people. The believers are mentioned because they are the principal component among them. Or it is connected to an implied element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) of "indecency," so the relative clause refers to the believers specifically; i.e., they love that indecency should occur concerning the believers and in their affair.

﴿for them﴾ because of what has been mentioned ﴿is a painful punishment in this world﴾ — the legal penalty (hadd) and other things from the worldly calamities that may befall them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) indeed applied the legal penalty for slander to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Hassan, and Mistah; and Safwan struck Hassan a blow with a sword and his sight was lost. (p-164) ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾ — from the punishment of the Fire and other things that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows.

﴿And Allah knows﴾ all matters, among which is what is in hearts of the aforementioned love ﴿while you do not know﴾ what Allah, exalted, knows. Rather, you only know what has become apparent to you of sayings and sensible actions. So base your affairs upon what you do, and punish in this world according to the outward conditions you witness; and Allah, glorified is He, is the one who takes charge of the hidden matters, so He will punish in the Hereafter for what the breasts conceal. This is when the painful punishment in this world is taken to mean the legal penalty for slander, or as encompassed by it, as the majority have agreed. But if it remains on its general meaning, with "love" meaning love itself without accompanying active pursuit of spreading it — which is the more fitting with the context of the noble composition — then the ordering of punishment upon it is a warning that the punishment of one who directly undertakes the spreading and takes charge of it is more severe and greater. And the parenthetical concluding interjection — I mean His saying, exalted: ﴿And Allah knows while you do not know﴾ — serves as confirmation of the establishment of the painful punishment for them and as its justification.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 20:

﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ is a repetition of the favour by not treating you with punishment, to draw attention to the utmost greatness of the offence.

﴿And that Allah is Kind (Ra'uf) and Merciful﴾ is a conjunction with ﴿the grace of Allah﴾. The use of the noble Name [Allah] is to cultivate awe and to convey that the attribute of divinity entails kindness and mercy. Its wording is altered and it is introduced with the particle of emphasis (inna) because the statement of His being, may He be exalted, characterised in His essence by ra'fah (tenderness), which is the perfection of mercy, and by al-Rahimiyyah (the Most Merciful), in which the intensity is continuous and constant, is not a statement of the occurrence of the connection of His tenderness and mercy to them. Likewise, the one meant by the conjoined element (al-ma'tuf 'alayhi) is the same, and the answer of "law la" (were it not) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 21:

﴿O you who have believed, do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾. That is: do not tread his paths in all that you do and all that you leave undone of the deeds, among which is spreading indecency and loving it. It is also read as "khutuwat" (khutuwāt) with the ṭāʼ (ṭāʼ) vocalized with a sukūn, and also with a fatḥa.

﴿And whoever follows the footsteps of Satan﴾. The apparent noun phrases have been placed in the position of their pronouns, where it did not say: "and whoever follows them," or "and whoever follows his footsteps," in order to increase the affirmation and to intensify the aversion and warning.

﴿Then indeed he commands indecency and wrongdoing﴾. This is a reason for the conditional consequence, placed in its position, as if it were said: "Then he has committed indecency and wrongdoing, because it is his constant habit to command both of them. So whoever follows his footsteps has certainly complied with his command." Indecency (fahshāʼ) is that whose ugliness is excessive, like the act of immorality (fāḥisha). Wrongdoing (munkar) is that which the Sharia disapproves of. The pronoun in "innahu" refers to Satan. It was also said that it refers to the matter (al-shaʼn), according to one who does not require the return of the pronoun in the consequent clause to the conditional noun; or that the original would be "yaʼmuruhu." It was also said that it refers back to "man" (whoever), meaning: that one who is followed commands people with both of them, because the nature of Satan is misguidance, so whoever follows him ascends from the rank of error and corruption to the rank of misguiding and corrupting.

﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾, through which are these clarifications, and the guidance to repentance that erases sins, and the prescribing of the prescribed punishments that expiate them.

﴿None of you would have ever been pure﴾. That is: would not have been cleansed of its defilement. It is also read as "mā zakkā" with shaddah, meaning: Allah the Exalted would not have purified [anyone].

The "min" in His saying ﴿of you﴾ is explanatory (bayāniyya), and the "min" in His saying (p-165) ﴿anyone﴾ is extra (zāʼida). "Aḥad" is in the position of nominative as the subject according to the first reading, and in the position of accusative as the object according to the second reading.

﴿Ever﴾: not to any end. ﴿But Allah purifies﴾: cleanses ﴿whom He wills﴾ of His servants, by adding the effects of His grace and mercy to repentance, then accepting it from them, as He did with you.

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾: emphatic in hearing the statements, among which is what they manifested of repentance.

﴿All-Knowing﴾: of all the things known, among which are their intentions. In this is an exhortation to them to be sincere in repentance. The manifestation of the noble Name is to signal that divinity requires hearing and knowledge, along with the emphasis on the independence of this concluding parenthetical remark.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 22:

﴿And let not those endowed with virtue (fadl) among you and wealth (sa'ah) swear⦆ — that is, let them not swear, from the root iftiʻal of al-ʼalliyyah (oath). It is also said: let them not fall short, from al-alw (falling short). The first is the more apparent, because it was revealed concerning al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr), may Allah be pleased with him, when he swore that he would no longer spend on Mistah, and he had been spending on him because he was the son of his maternal aunt and was among the poor emigrants (muhajirun). It is supported by the reading of one who recited: "wa la yatalla" (and let him not swear).

﴿Those endowed with virtue among you﴾ — in religion. And that is sufficient as evidence for the virtue of al-Siddiq, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him.

﴿And those of wealth﴾ — in property. ﴿That they should give﴾ — that is, "that they should not give" (understood by 'an la, "not"), or it is read with the second-person form by way of iltifat (shift of person).

﴿To the near of kin, the needy, and the emigrants in the way of Allah﴾ — these are descriptions of one single referent, brought in by way of conjunction, to draw attention to the fact that each of them is an independent cause for entitlement to being given. It is also said: they are descriptions of several referents, which stand in their place; and the second object has been omitted because it is so evident, that is: "that they should not give them anything."

﴿And let them pardon﴾ what has proceeded from them, ﴿and let them overlook﴾ it by turning away from it. Both imperatives have been read with the second-person ta' (taʼ al-khitab), in accordance with the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Do you not love that Allah should forgive you?﴾ — that is, in return for your pardoning, your overlooking, and your kindness to one who has wronged you.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ — exceedingly so in forgiveness and mercy, along with His complete power to call to account and the abundance of the sins that call for it. In this is a great exhortation to pardon and a generous promise of reward for it, as if it were said: "Do you not love that Allah should forgive you?" — and this is one of its requirements. It is related that he (ﷺ) recited it to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "Yes, I love that Allah should forgive me," and he returned to Mistah his maintenance, and said: "By Allah, I will never withdraw it."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 23:

﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste women﴾ i.e., those who are pure from what they have been accused of, of unchastity, ﴿heedless﴾ of it entirely, such that nothing of it, nor of its preliminaries, has ever come to their minds at all. In this there is an indication of perfect purity that is not found in "the believing women" (al-muhsanat), i.e., those whose breasts are sound and whose hearts are God-fearing, guarded against every evil.

﴿Believing﴾ i.e., those characterized by faith in everything that must be believed in, of obligations and prohibitions and other things, with true, detailed faith, as the delaying of "believing women" after what precedes it indicates, despite the originality of the attribute of faith. For this indicates that what is meant by it is the descriptive sense that expresses what has been mentioned, not the nominal sense that validates the application of the name in general, as is apparent under the assumption of the preceding. What is meant by them is 'A'isha al-Siddiqa, may Allah be pleased with her, and the plural is in consideration of the fact that her accusation is an accusation against all the Mothers of the Believers, since all share in infallibility, purity, and belonging to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ and its like. It has also been said: the Mothers of the Believers, so al-Siddiqa enters among them by primary inclusion. As for what has been said, that what is meant is al-Siddiqa and the plural is in consideration of her including the women of the community who possess the mentioned attributes, this is rejected by the fact that the punishments consequent upon accusing these women are punishments specific to the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and there is no doubt that accusing women other than the Mothers of the Believers is not disbelief. Therefore, what must be meant is them, on one of the two views, for they have been singled out from among all the believing women, so their accusation was made disbelief, to manifest their honor with Allah, mighty and majestic, and to protect the sanctuary of prophethood from anyone approaching it with evil. So much so that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, considered it more severe than the rest of the forms of disbelief when asked about these verses, and he said: "Whoever commits a sin and then repents of it, his repentance is accepted, except for whoever engaged in the matter of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her." Was it, then, from him, may Allah be pleased with him, except to magnify the matter of the slander and to alert that it is a grave disbelief.

﴿They are cursed﴾ for what they said concerning them ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾, where they are cursed by those who curse them among the believers and the angels forever. ﴿And for them﴾, in addition to the everlasting curse mentioned, ﴿is a great punishment﴾, terrible, whose extent cannot be measured, due to the extreme magnitude of the crime they committed.

The phrase "on the Day when it bears witness against them" (﴿يَوْمَ تَشْهَدُ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾) and what follows could either be connected to what precedes it or be separate from it.

If it is connected to what precedes, it is brought to confirm the punishment mentioned, by specifying the time of its arrival and making it awe-inspiring, through a statement of how their offences, which necessitate that punishment, become manifest together with all their other offences, which bring their own punishments, in a terrifying manner and an appearance that breaks customary norms. In that case, "yawma" (يَوْمَ, "on the day") is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) of what is in the preceding prepositional phrase (al-jār wa al-majrūr) in the sense of "being fixed" or "established." It is not an adverbial complement of "punishment" ('adhāb). Although we set aside the description of this, because it disrupts the eloquence of the meaning.

If it is separate from what precedes it, it is brought to magnify the Day by magnifying what it contains. It is an adverbial complement of a delayed verb which has been deliberately omitted, to signal that expression falls short of detailing what occurs in it of the overwhelming catastrophe and the universal calamity. It is as if it were said: "On the day their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do" there will be, of the states and terrors, what no description can encompass.

Moreover, the relative pronoun mentioned (al-mawṣūl, "what") refers to all their evil deeds and abominable offences, not only to their well-known offences alone.

The meaning of the bodily members bearing witness with these is that God makes them speak by His power, so that each limb reports what proceeded from it of its owner's actions. It does not mean that each of them reports only their well-known offences. The relative pronoun and the omitted element refer to these actions and to all the varieties of punishments that follow from them, not to one of the two alone. Therefore, it contains of the kinds of magnification, both in summary and in detail, what admits no addition.

To restrict the relative pronoun to the specific well-known offences, and to take the bearing witness of the limbs to mean only the reporting of all of them concerning those offences, is to confine what is broad and to diminish the matter of the restraint.

The combination of the past and the future verb forms serves to indicate their continuance in these deeds in this world. The placing of "ʿalayhim" (عَلَيْهِمْ, "against them") before the subject serves to hasten to show that the testimony is harmful to them, together with what this carries of suspense toward the delayed element, as has been mentioned many times.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On that Day Allah will pay them their due recompense in full﴾. That is: on the day when their limbs bear witness to their ugly deeds, Allah the Exalted will give them their recompense, the established one, which is certain to befall them without doubt, complete and full. This is a new sentence, brought to explain the order of the judgment concerning that witnessing, and it includes, in summary form, an explanation of the vague element that was omitted. It is also permissible for "the day when they bear witness" (yawma yashhadu) to be a time adverb governing "He will pay them" (yuwaffihim), with "that Day" (yawma'idhin) in apposition to it. It has been said that it is in the accusative as the object of a hidden verb, meaning: "Remember the day when they bear witness," with the verb in the imperative form for emphasis.

﴿And they will know﴾ at the moment of witnessing the terrors and calamities, as the Noble Qur'an has declared.

﴿that Allah is the Truth﴾, the Established One who is worthy to be established without doubt in His essence, His attributes, and His acts, among which are His perfect words, which inform about the matters they are witnessing, corresponding exactly to them.

﴿the Manifest﴾: the One who makes things manifest as they are in themselves. Or it means: the One whose truth is evident. Interpreting it as the manifestation of His divinity, the absence of any partner in it, and the inability of anything else to grant reward or punishment, is not very relevant to the context, just as interpreting "the Truth" as "the Possessor of clear right," meaning the Just whose justice is evident, is not. Likewise, if you were to survey the verses of threat in the Glorious Criterion (al-Furqan al-Majid) that are directed against every rebellious disbeliever and stubborn tyrant, you would find none of them surpassing those thunderclaps filled with various kinds of warning and severity. This is only to show the exalted rank of the Prophet (ﷺ) in loftiness of station and distinction, and to display the high standing of al-Siddiqa (the Truthful), may Allah be pleased with her, in chastity and purity.

And His saying, ﴿The wicked women are for wicked men﴾ and so on, is a resumed statement, driven by the divine custom that operates among creatures, on the basis that God Most High has an angel who drives each kind to its own kind. That is: the wicked women ﴿are for the wicked men﴾, meaning they are specific to them and do not tend to go beyond them to others, with the lam (اللَّامُ, lam al-ikhtisas, the lam of exclusivity) indicating specificity.

﴿And the wicked men are for the wicked women﴾ likewise, because similarity is among the causes of union.

﴿And the good women﴾ among them ﴿are for the good men﴾ also among them, ﴿and the good men are for the good women﴾ likewise, in such a way that they hardly go beyond them to anyone else. Since the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was the best of the best and the choicest of the first and the last, it becomes clear by necessity that al-Siddiqah (the Truthful one, may God be pleased with her) is among the best of the good women, and the falsehood of the fabrications said about her becomes evident, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾. The demonstrative (أُولَئِكَ) refers primarily to the People of the House, who include al-Siddiqah in the first place. It has also been said that it refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), al-Siddiqah, and Safwan. The "ma" (مَا) in the demonstrative carries the sense of distance, to indicate the lofty rank of those referred to and the remoteness of their station in virtue; that is: those described by lofty standing are cleared of the lies that the people of the slander fabricated about them.

It has also been said: the wicked speech is specific to the wicked men and women, meaning it is proper to them and fitting for them alone and should not be said about anyone else. Likewise, the wicked among both groups are deserving that wicked speech be said about them. The good words are specific to and truly belong to the good among both groups, and they are deserving that good words be said about them. ﴿Those, the good, are cleared of what the wicked say about them﴾; its outcome is therefore also the exoneration of al-Siddiqah.

It has also been said: the wicked speech is specific to the wicked among the two groups, not issuing from anyone else; the wicked among both groups are specialised in wicked speech and exposed to it; and the good speech is for the good among both groups, meaning it is specific to them and does not issue from anyone else; the good among both groups are specialised in good speech, from which nothing else issues. ﴿Those, the good, are cleared of what the wicked say﴾ of the wickedness (مِنَ الخَبائِثِ), meaning such things do not issue from them. Its outcome is therefore the exoneration of those who said: ﴿Glory be to You, this is a tremendous slander﴾.

﴿For them is forgiveness﴾, great forgiveness, for what humankind is never free of, namely sins.

﴿And a noble provision﴾, which is Paradise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 27:

﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own houses﴾ Following what was detailed concerning fornication (zina) and concerning the accusation of chaste women regarding it, the discussion turns to detailing the restraints against what may lead to either of them: the mingling of men and women, and men entering upon women at times of privacy (khalwat), and the teaching of beautiful manners (adab) and pleasing conduct that results in the happiness of both abodes. The description of the houses as "other than your houses" comes out in the customary sense, which is that each person dwells in his own property. Otherwise, the one who rents and the one who lends are also prohibited from entering without permission. It was also read: "biyutan ghayra biyutikum" (بِيُوتًا غَيْرَ بِيُوتِكُمْ), with a kasra on the ba' (بِيُوتًا) for the sake of the following ya' (ياء).

﴿until you seek permission (tasta'nisu)﴾ That is: you seek permission from the one who holds the authority to grant it from its owners. It derives from al-istina's (الاستئناس) in the sense of al-isti'lam (الاستعلام, seeking knowledge or information), from anisa al-shay' (انس الشيء), meaning when he perceived it; for the one seeking permission (al-musta'nis) seeks to know the situation and to discover whether he will be permitted. Or it derives from al-istina's (الاستئناس), which is the opposite of al-istiwhash (الاستيحاش, feeling of estrangement), because the one asking permission feels estranged and fears that he will not be permitted; so when he is permitted, he becomes at ease (ista'nasa).

﴿and greet its inhabitants (tusallimu 'ala ahliha)﴾ at the time of seeking permission. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that the greeting is that one says: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" three times; if he is permitted, he enters, and otherwise he returns.

﴿That is best for you﴾ That is, seeking permission together with the greeting is better for you than entering suddenly, or upon the greeting of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance), where a man among them, when he wished to enter a house other than his own, would say: "Good morning to you, good evening to you," and then enter; so perhaps a man would find himself with his wife under a blanket. It is also related that a man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Should I seek permission to enter upon my mother?" He said: "Yes." He said: "She has no servant other than me; should I seek permission to enter upon her every time I enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Would you like to see her naked?" He said: "No." He (ﷺ) said: "Then seek permission."

﴿so that you may remember﴾ This is connected to an implied verb, meaning: you were commanded with it, or it was said to you, this so that you may remember, take admonition, and act in accordance with its requirement.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 28:

﴿And if you do not find anyone therein﴾: that is, anyone who possesses the permission to admit you. This is on the understanding that one who does not possess it, whether women or children, is as good as absent, since finding them is the same as not finding them. Or it means: not anyone at all. On this reading, the explicit meaning (ʿibārat al-naṣṣ) of the noble text is a prohibition on entering empty houses, because of what it involves of looking into matters that people customarily keep hidden. Moreover, interfering with another's property is forbidden absolutely. As for the prohibition on entering houses in which there are women and children, it is established by implication (dalālat al-naṣṣ, the sense understood from the text's underlying reason without being stated explicitly). This is because entry is forbidden where the stated reason exists, so it is all the more forbidden when something stronger than that reason is added to it, namely looking upon what is private (ʿawrāt). Looking upon the private parts is more deserving of prohibition.

﴿So do not enter them﴾ and be patient, ﴿until permission is given to you﴾: that is, by the one who has the authority to grant permission, when he comes. As for "whoever" (man), he explained it by saying: "until one comes who gives you permission," or "until you find someone who gives you permission." Thus he presented the definite (al-qaṭʿī) in the form of a possibility. Since making the prohibition conditional on permission might give the impression that waiting at the doors is permitted in every case, he removed this by saying: 

﴿And if it is said to you, "Go back," then go back﴾: that is, if you are ordered by the people of the house to return, whether the order comes from someone who has the authority to grant permission or not at first, then go back. Do not insist by repeating the request for permission, as in the first case, and do not enter by persisting in waiting until the one who grants permission comes, as in the second case. For this kind of persistence brings resentment into people's hearts and damages one's dignity (murūwah) to a great degree.

﴿That﴾, i.e., going back, ﴿is purer for you﴾: that is, more pure than the stubbornness, obstinacy and standing at the doors, which are never free of the filth of baseness and vileness.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of what you do﴾: so He knows what you do and what you leave undone of what you have been charged with, and He will reward you for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 29:

﴿There is no blame upon you for entering﴾ i.e., without seeking permission, ﴿houses not inhabited﴾ i.e., houses not established for the habitation of a particular group only, but in which anyone who has need of them may take benefit, whoever he may be, without making them a dwelling, such as inns (rubut), caravanserais (khanat), shops (hawanit), bathhouses (hammamat) and the like, for these are prepared for the interests of people in general, as indicated by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿wherein is provision (mata') for you﴾. For this phrase is an attribute of the houses, or it is a resumptive clause functioning as a justification for the absence of blame, i.e., in them there is a right of enjoyment for you, such as shelter from heat and cold, storing goods and men, buying and selling, bathing, and other things that befit the condition of houses and their interiors. So there is no harm in entering them without seeking permission from their occupants beforehand, nor from those who manage their affairs and oversee their administration, such as the keepers of the caravanserais and inns, the owners of the shops, the operators of the bathhouses, and the like.

It is narrated that "Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: O Messenger of Allah, Allah, Exalted is He, has revealed to you a verse concerning seeking permission, and we engage in trade and lodge in these inns; should we not enter them except with permission? So it was revealed." It has also been said: these are the ruined houses in which one relieves oneself, and mata' means relieving oneself. The apparent meaning, however, is that these are among the category encompassed by "houses," not that they alone are intended.

And His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾ are a warning to whoever enters any of these places for corruption or for spying upon private matters (awrat).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 30:

﴿Say to the believing men﴾ This begins the explanation of general rulings encompassing all the believers, within which the ruling concerning those who seek permission when entering houses falls as a primary inclusion. The shift of address and its direction to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the delegation of the commands and prohibitions within its scope to his (ﷺ) judgment, are because these are obligations related to many particular matters that occur frequently, such that the one who issues them and who takes charge of arranging them should truly be a guardian and overseer over them. The object of the command is another command that has been omitted, relying on the indication of its response, i.e.: "Say to them: lower [your gaze]."

﴿that they lower their gaze﴾ from what is forbidden, and restrict themselves to what is lawful, ﴿and guard their private parts﴾ except from their spouses or what their right hands possess. The restriction of lowering the gaze with the partitive "min" (some of), in contrast to guarding, is due to the latitude present in the matter of looking. It has also been said that what is meant by guarding here specifically is concealment.

﴿That﴾ i.e., what has been mentioned of lowering the gaze and guarding, ﴿is purer for them﴾ i.e., it is cleaner for them from the filth of suspicion.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do﴾ Nothing is hidden from Him of what proceeds from them of deeds, among which are the roving of the gaze, the use of all the senses, and the movement of the limbs, and what they intend by these. So let them be wary of Him in everything they do and everything they leave undone.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 31:

﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze from their sight﴾, so that they do not look at what it is not lawful for them to look at. ﴿And guard their private parts﴾ by concealment or by preserving them from adultery. The mention of lowering the gaze first is because looking leads to adultery, and looking is the lure of corruption.

﴿And not display their adornment﴾ such as jewelry and other things with which one adorns oneself. In it there is exaggeration in forbidding the exposure of its places, which is not hidden.

﴿Except what appears of it﴾ in the course of carrying out matters that are customarily unavoidable, such as the ring, kohl, henna and the like, for there is hardship among us in concealing them. It has been said: the meaning of "adornment" is its places, with an omitted noun (idafa), or that it encompasses both innate beauty and adornment. The exception is the face and the two palms, because they are not 'awrah.

﴿And let them draw their head-coverings over their chests﴾: this is guidance on how to conceal some places of adornment after the prohibition of displaying them. The women used, in the manner of the Jahiliyya, to throw their head-coverings behind them, so their necks and necklaces would show from their open collars. So they were commanded to let their head-coverings fall over their collars as a covering for what would otherwise appear. The verb "yadribna" has been given the sense of "ilqa" (casting), so it takes "ala". It is also read with a kasra on the jim, as previously mentioned.

﴿And not display their adornment﴾: the prohibition is repeated in order to make an exception of some of the matters of permission from it, from the viewpoint of the one who looks, after some of the matters of necessity were excepted from it, from the viewpoint of what is looked at.

﴿Except to their husbands﴾, for they are the ones for whom adornment is intended, and they may look at all of her body, even the customary place.

﴿Or their fathers, or the fathers of their husbands, or their sons, or the sons of their husbands, or their brothers, or the sons of their brothers, or the sons of their sisters﴾: because of the necessary frequent association between them and women, and the scarcity of expected temptation from them, due to the natural aversion of both sides to intimacy with close relatives. They may look at what appears of women during service and work. The paternal and maternal uncles are not mentioned, because it is more cautious for women to cover themselves from them, lest they describe them to their sons.

﴿Or their women﴾: those specifically associated with them through companionship and service, from among free believing women, for unbelieving women do not refrain from describing them to men.

﴿Or what their right hands possess﴾: that is, of the female slaves, for a woman's male slave is in the position of a non-mahram man to her. It has been said: of the female slaves and male slaves, on the basis of what is related: "He ﷺ came to Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, with a slave he had given her, and she was wearing a garment which, when she covered her head with it, did not reach her feet, and when she covered her feet, did not reach her head. He ﷺ said: 'There is no harm for you; he is only your father and your servant.'"

﴿Or male attendants who have no physical desire﴾: that is, those who have need of women. These are the impotent old men, and those who are castrated or the eunuch, which is a matter of disagreement. It has been said they are the simpletons who follow people for the sake of their food and understand nothing of women's affairs. It is also read as "ghayra" in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (hal).

﴿Or children who have not yet become aware of women's private matters﴾: either because they do not yet discern, with "zuhur" meaning "ittila'" (becoming aware), or because they have not reached the limit of desire, with "zuhur" meaning "ghalaba" (overpowering). "Tifl" is a generic noun placed in the position of the plural, being sufficient by the indication of the attribute.

﴿And let them not stamp their feet so as to reveal what they conceal of their adornment﴾: that is, what they conceal of it from sight. ﴿Of their adornment﴾: that is, let them not strike the ground with their feet so that their anklets clink, and so it is known that they wear anklets, for that causes men to incline toward them and gives the impression that they have an inclination toward them. In forbidding the display of the sound of jewelry after forbidding the display of its substance, there is an exaggeration in deterring the exposure of its places which is not hidden.

﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you﴾: a shift in address, turning it away from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to everyone by way of predominance, to show the complete concern with the matter of repentance contained within this context, and that it is among the greatest of important matters, fitting that He, glory be to Him and exalted, is the one who commands it, since hardly anyone among the responsible persons is free from some kind of shortcoming in properly fulfilling the obligations of the duties. Enough is his ﷺ saying: "Surah Hud has made me grey," because of what it contains of His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾, especially when what is commanded is restraint from desires. It has been said: repent from what you used to do in the Jahiliyya, for although it was obligatory to repent upon Islam, it is obligatory to feel regret for it and resolve to abandon it whenever it occurs to one's mind. The repetition of the address with His saying, exalted be He: ﴿O you who believe﴾ is an emphasis on the obligation and an announcement that the attribute of faith necessitates compliance definitively. It is also read "ayyuhu al-mu'minuna".

﴿So that you may succeed﴾: that you may win thereby the happiness of both abodes.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 32:

﴿And marry off the single among you﴾ After the Exalted had forbidden fornication and its beginnings, both near and remote, He commanded marriage. For marriage, although it is intended in itself insofar as it is the means of preserving the species, is the best deterrent from that. The word "ayama" (singles) is an inversion of "ayaymu," the plural of "ayyim," which denotes whoever has no spouse, whether man or woman, virgin or previously married, as the saying of the one who said makes clear:

"If you marry, I shall marry, and if you remain single, I too shall remain single, though I am more worthy of being single than you."

That is: marry off those among free men and free women who have no spouse.

﴿And the righteous among your male slaves and your female slaves﴾ on the basis that the address is to guardians and masters. The consideration of righteousness applies to slaves because one who lacks righteousness among them is far from being deserving that his master should attend to his affairs, bear hardship for him, or exert himself in arranging his interests with what is necessary, legally and customarily, of spending wealth and benefits; rather, his due is that the master keep him for himself. As for the lack of consideration of righteousness in free men and free women, it is because righteousness is generally found among them, and because they have authority over their own dispositions and their property. So when they resolve to marry, the guardians must assist them, since there is no burden upon them in this matter such that a gain returning to them, immediate or deferred, should be weighed against it. It has also been said: the intended meaning is readiness for marriage and fulfilling its rights.
