﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾ as a removal of what might be an obstacle to marriage from the poverty of either party. That is: let not the poverty of the suitor or of the betrothed prevent the marriage, for in the bounty of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, there is sufficiency beyond wealth; He goes forth and returns, and provides for whom He wills from where he does not reckon. Or it is a promise from Him, glorified is He, of enrichment, in accordance with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Seek wealth through this verse." Yet it is conditional upon His will, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills﴾.

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, Rich and possessed of abundance, whose enriching of creatures does not diminish Him, since His blessing has no end and His power has no limit despite that.

﴿All-Knowing﴾, who expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it as wisdom and interest require.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 33:**

﴿And let those who cannot find the means of marriage keep themselves chaste﴾. This is guidance for those unable to meet the beginnings and means of marriage, directing them to what is better and more fitting for them, after the permissibility of marrying the poor has been stated. That is: let him strive for chastity and for suppressing desire.

﴿Those who cannot find the means of marriage﴾, that is, they lack the means of marriage at first and are not able to obtain the wealth with which marriage is contracted.

﴿Until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾. This is a generous promise of Allah's favour in granting them wealth, a kindness to them in their chastity, a strengthening of their hearts, and a notice that His bounty, exalted is He, is more deserving of their abstinence and closer than the righteous.

﴿And those who seek a writing﴾. After commanding the marrying off of the righteous slaves who are entitled to be married, He commanded the writing of a contract of manumission (mukatabah) for those among them who would deserve it. The word kitab (writing) is a verbal noun from kataba, like mukatabah. That is: those who seek a mukatabah.

﴿From among those whom your right hands possess﴾, whether male slave or female slave. Mukatabah is that the master says to his slave: "I contract with you for such-and-such a sum of dirhams, which you will pay to me, and you will be freed," and the slave says: "I accept," or words to that effect. If he pays it to him, he is freed. The scholars said: its meaning is: "I have written upon myself that you will be freed by me when you fulfil the money, and you have written upon yourself that you will fulfil this," or "I have written upon you the fulfilment of the money, and I have written upon myself the freeing at its completion."

The verification is that mukatabah is a name for the contract that results from the combination of their two statements, like all legitimate contracts concluded by offer and acceptance. There is no doubt that this does not truly arise except from the two contracting parties, and the function of each of them in reality is only to bring one of its two halves, expressing what is completed from his side and what proceeds from him of his own act, without addressing what is completed from the side of his companion and proceeds from his act. However, since each of those two acts cannot be realized in itself except when dependent on the realization of the other, because the master's undertaking to free in exchange for the payment cannot be conceived of being realized except with the slave's undertaking to pay, just as the contract of sale, which is the transfer of ownership of the sold item for the price on the part of the seller, cannot be realized by his owning the price on the part of the buyer, it was necessary that each of them include the other at the time of the concluding. Thus, just as the seller's saying "I have sold" is a concluding of the contract of sale, in the sense that it is an effecting of what is completed from his side primarily, and of what is completed from the side of the buyer implicitly, an effecting that depends on the buyer's opinion, a dependence resembling the dependence of an unauthorized contract (fudul), so too the master's saying "I have contracted you for such-and-such" is a concluding of the contract of mukatabah, that is, an effecting of what is completed from his side, namely the undertaking to free in exchange for the payment primarily, and of what is completed from the side of the slave, namely the undertaking of the payment implicitly, an effecting that depends on his acceptance. When it is accepted, the contract is complete.

The place of the relative clause is nominative as the subject, its predicate being ﴿then write to them﴾, and the fa' is because it includes the meaning of a condition. Or it is accusative, as an object of a hidden verb that this explains. The imperative here is for recommendation (nadb), because mukatabah is a contract that includes kindness, so it is not obligatory like others. It is permissible to be immediate, deferred, in instalments, or not in instalments. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, it is not permissible except deferred, in both respects. This has been detailed in its proper place.

﴿If you know good in them﴾, that is: trustworthiness, right conduct, and the ability to pay the sum by earning it through a lawful means, and their being fit so that they will not harm people after being freed and given free rein.

﴿And give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾. This is a command to the ruler (wali) to give some of their wealth. Included in its ruling is the remission of some of the mukatabah money, and the least amount that is considered wealth suffices for that. From Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: the remission of a quarter. From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: a third. This is for recommendation according to us, but according to al-Shafi'i it is obligatory. What refutes this is his, peace be upon him, saying: "The mukatabah is a slave as long as a single dirham remains upon him," for if remission were obligatory, the remainder would drop from him absolutely. Also, if remission were obligatory, its obligation would be linked to the contract, so the contract would both obligate and cancel at once. Also, it is a contract of exchange, so one is not compelled to remit, as in sale. It was said: the meaning of "give them" is "lend to them." It was said: it is a command to them to spend on them after they have paid and been freed. The attribution of the wealth to Him, exalted is He, and the description of it as what He has given them, is to incite obedience to the command by realizing what is commanded, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾. For noticing that the wealth reaches them from His side, while He is the true owner of it, is one of the strongest motives for spending it on the direction commanded. It was said: it is a command to give them their share of the alms, so the command is obligatory without exception, and the attribution and description are to specify the source. It was said: it is a command of recommendation for all Muslims to help the mukatabs by giving charity to them. This is permissible for the master even if he is rich, because the description has changed, as is indicated by the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in the hadith of Barira: "It is a charity for her and a gift for us."

﴿And do not compel your female slaves﴾, that is, your maidservants. Both fata (young man) and fatah (young woman) are well-known metaphors for male slave and female slave. Upon this is based his, peace be upon him, saying: "Let one of you say 'my young man' and 'my young woman,' and let him not say 'my slave' and 'my slave-girl.'" This expression in this context, considering its original meaning, has a good fit and further suitability to His saying: ﴿to prostitution﴾, which is fornication, insofar as it comes from women, because they are the ones from whom it is generally expected, rather than the old women or the young girls.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿if they desire chastity﴾ is not to restrict the prohibition to the case of their desiring to abstain from fornication, excluding what is other than it from its ruling, as when the compulsion is because of their dislike of fornication with a particular man, or at a particular time, or in a particular place, or for other such matters that generally justify compulsion. Rather, it is to preserve their continuous custom, for they used to compel them to prostitution while they wished to abstain from it, along with the strength of their desire commanding them to debauchery and their deficiency in knowing the matters that call to good and restrain from vile deeds. For Abdullah ibn Ubayy had six slave-girls whom he compelled to fornication and imposed levies upon them. Two of them complained to the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, and this was revealed. In this there is an added reproach to their condition and a condemnation of their vile conduct, which is not hidden. For whoever has even a little manliness can hardly be content with the debauchery of those in his household among his female slaves, let alone commanding them to it or compelling them to it, especially if they desire chastity. So reflect, and leave aside what has been said: that this is because compulsion is not possible except with the desire for chastity; and what has been said: that if it is made a condition for the prohibition, it does not follow from its absence that compulsion is permitted, since it is possible that the lifting of the prohibition is due to the impossibility of the forbidden thing. For both of these are far from verification. The choice of the word "if" (in) rather than "when" (idha), although the desire is certainly realized in the case of the text, is for notifying that it is obligatory to refrain from compulsion when the desire for chastity is in the realm of doubt and uncertainty, so how much more so when it is certainly occurring, as is the actual case? And its explanation by saying that the stated desire from them is in the realm of the rare and unusual, together with its being entirely without benefit, is contradicted by considering its realization as a clear refusal.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in order to seek the transient goods of this worldly life﴾ is a qualification of the compulsion, but not in the sense that it is the basis of the prohibition against it. Rather, it is in the sense that it is what was customary among them, as it was accepted by them, to reproach them for what they were doing of risking a great burden for the sake of a paltry gain. That is: do not do what you are doing of compelling them to prostitution in pursuit of fleeting enjoyment that will soon vanish. So what is meant by seeking here is the seeking that accompanies the attainment of the sought object and its enjoyment in action, since that alone is suitable for being the aim of the compulsion, consequent upon it, and not the general seeking that includes the prior request that prompts it.

﴿And whoever compels them﴾, and so on, is a new sentence brought to confirm the prohibition and to emphasise the obligation to act upon it, by explaining that the compelled women are freed from the punishment of the one compelled to it, in expression, and that the harm of compulsion returns to the compellers, in allusion. That is: whoever compels them to what has been mentioned of prostitution, ﴿then Allah, after their being compelled, is Forgiving, Merciful﴾. That is: toward them, as it occurs in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, and upon it is the reading of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, and as His saying, ﴿after their being compelled﴾ indicates, that is, their state of being compelled. Furthermore, compulsion is a verbal noun from the passive voice, for placing it between the subject of inna and its predicate indicates that this is the cause of forgiveness and mercy. Al-Hasan al-Basri, may Allah have mercy on him, used to say when he recited this verse: "For them, by Allah, for them, by Allah." Restricting these two to them and determining their basis, together with the prior mention of the compellers in the conditional clause, is clear evidence that the compellers are wholly deprived of both, as if it were said: "not for the one compelled," and since this supposition is evident, it suffices in place of a pronoun referring back to the conditional word. So permitting that the two attach to the compellers on condition of repentance, independently, or along with the compelled women, would disrupt the eloquence of the sublime arrangement and make light of the prohibition in a context of dread, and it would indicate the women's need for forgiveness, which points to a prior sin, either by considering that they, although compelled, are not free of some element of compliance with what human nature requires within acts of fornication, or by considering that compulsion may fall short of the limit of coercion that completely removes choice, or to emphasise the enormity of the matter of fornication and to urge the compelled women to hold firm in avoiding it, and to be severe in warning the compellers by showing that the women, while they were exposed to punishment were it not for forgiveness and mercy covering them, with the excuse of compulsion existing on their behalf, then what is the state of whoever compels them, in deserving punishment?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 34:

﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses that make things clear﴾. This is an independent statement, introduced amid the verses preceding and following it, to show the great significance of these matters, which call for wholehearted application to acting upon their content. It is introduced with the oath which the lam expresses, to highlight the complete care given to this matter. That is: By Allah, We have certainly sent down to you this noble surah as verses that make clear everything you need clarified of the hudud (prescribed penalties), the other rulings, the adab (good conduct), and other matters that are among the principles of its clarification. The attribution of making clear to them is metaphorical. Or [the meaning is]: verses that are evident, which are confirmed by the earlier scriptures and sound intellects. And "mubayyinat" may be from bayyana in the sense of tabayyana (become clear), as in the proverb: "The dawn has become clear to one who has two eyes." It has also been read in the passive form, meaning: those which have been made clear and explained in this surah of the meanings of the rulings and the hudud. It has also been permitted that the original sense is "explaining the rulings within them," and so the adverbial phrase was extended by treating it as an object.

﴿And an example from those who passed away before you﴾. This is coordinated with "verses" — that is: and We have sent down an example of the kind of the examples of those who passed away before you, from the wondrous stories and the parables struck for them in the earlier scriptures and the words that were spoken by the tongues of the Prophets, peace be upon them. This includes the story of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, which parallels the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the story of Maryam, may Allah be pleased with her, and the other examples occurring in the noble surah, clearly arranged. Restricting the clear verses to the earlier ones and taking the example to mean only the wondrous story is rejected by the sequel of the discourse with the illustrations that will come.

﴿And an admonition﴾ by which you are admonished and restrained from what is not fitting of the forbidden and the disliked and all else that disturbs the excellences of good conduct. It is thus an expression for what has preceded of verses and examples, because it is evident that they are admonitions in the sense mentioned. (p-175) The basis of the coordination is the difference in designation, which is treated as if it were a difference in essence. The verses have been specified for what makes clear the hudud and rulings, and the admonition for what was admonished by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let not pity for them take hold of you in the religion of Allah﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did you not say﴾, and other verses occurring concerning matters of good conduct. The phrase ﴿for the God-fearing﴾ was said although the admonition is general to all, in accordance with the generality of the sending down in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have sent down to you﴾, as an incitement to the addressees to take care to be enrolled among the God-fearing, by showing that they are the ones who benefit from its effects and draw from its lights alone. It has been said: what is meant by the clear verses, the example, and the admonition is everything in the Glorious Qur'an of verses, examples, and admonitions.

Then his saying, ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ and so on. Here it is a resumptive clause (istinaf, a new sentence that continues the discourse without grammatical attachment), brought to affirm the clarity (bayan) contained in it, while indicating that this clarity is at the highest degree of perfection in the manner you will come to know. As for the first reading, it is to establish that His clarification, may He be exalted, is not restricted to what is mentioned in this noble surah, but encompasses everything whose clarification is due: the rulings and laws, their principles and their ends that result from them in this world and the Hereafter, and other matters that have a role in clarification. It also establishes that this clarification proceeds from Him, may He be exalted, in the most complete and perfect manner, since He expressed it by "illumination" (tanwir), which is the strongest and most manifest level of clarification. He expressed the one who illuminates by the very term "light" (nur), to draw attention to the strength of the illumination and the intensity of its effect, and to inform that He, may He be exalted, is manifest in His own essence, and everything other than Him is manifest by His manifesting it, just as light is luminous in its own essence and whatever else is illuminated by it. The light is attributed to the heavens and the earth to show the complete pervasiveness of the clarification borrowed for it and the utmost comprehensiveness of its reach to everything fitting for it among the matters that have a role in guiding people, through the mediation of the all-encompassing scope of that from which the metaphor is borrowed, to everything that the heavens and the earth receive and deserve of the upper and lower bodies, for they are the two poles of the corporeal world, for which there is no manifestation of sensory light other than them. Or it refers to the comprehensiveness of the clarification regarding their conditions and the conditions of what is in them of existent things, since there is no existent thing except that some of its conditions have been clarified, whether in detail or in summary. How could it not be so, when there is no doubt that its being a proof of the existence of the Creator and His attributes, and a witness to the validity of resurrection, is clear? Or it refers to the clarification being connected to their inhabitants, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "the guide of the people of the heavens and the earth; they are guided by His light, and by His guidance they escape the bewilderment of misguidance." This is what is said. As for interpreting "illumination" as His bringing quiddities (mahiyyat, the realities of things) from non-existence into existence, since that is the origin of manifestation just as annihilation is the origin of concealment; or as the adornment of the heavens with the two luminaries and the rest of the stars and what emanates from them of lights, or with the angels, peace be upon them; and the adornment of the earth with the prophets, peace be upon them, the scholars and the believers; or with plants and trees; or as His management of their affairs and the affairs of what is in them, then these do not suit the context nor support the excellence of the arrangement.

﴿The parable of His light﴾ that is, His light which overflows from Him, may He be exalted, upon the things illuminated by it, and it is the Qur'an that clarifies, as what precedes it indicates by describing His verses with revelation and clarification. He has also explicitly stated that it is light in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾. This is also what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Aslam, may Allah have mercy on them all, said. Some have taken it to be an expression for the Truth, although the borrowing of light for the Truth is common, as the borrowing of darkness for falsehood is. But this is rejected by the context of describing the status of the verses and their attributes, with what has been mentioned of clarification, while the Truth has not been previously mentioned. Also, what is considered in the concept of light is manifestation and making manifest, as is the case with the noble Qur'an; whereas what is considered in the concept of the Truth, insofar as it is the Truth, is being manifest, not making manifest. The meaning of "parable" (mathal) here is the wondrous attribute, that is, the wondrous attribute of His light.

﴿like a niche﴾ that is, like the description of a window (kuwwah) piercing a wall, in terms of its giving light and illumination.

﴿within which is a lamp﴾: a large, piercing lamp. It is said that the mishkah (niche) is the tube in the middle of the lamp-stand, and the misbah (lamp) is the burning wick.

﴿The lamp is in a glass﴾ that is, in a lamp-stand of pure, bright glass. It has been recited with a fath and a kasra on the zay in both places.

﴿The glass is as if it were a brilliant star﴾ sparkling, blazing, resembling a pearl in its clarity and brightness. "Durri" (brilliant) refers to the large well-known stars. It has been recited as "durri'" with a kasra on the dal, a shaddah on the ra, and a long ya followed by a hamzah, as an intensive form (fa'il) from al-dar', which means repelling, that is, it is intensive in repelling darkness by its light, or in repelling some parts of its light from others at the time of its flashing and sparkling. It has also been recited with a damma on the dal, while the rest remains as it is. The repetition of "the lamp" and "the glass" in definite form, after their having been mentioned in indefinite form, and the reporting about them by what follows, with the coherence of the sentence being maintained such that it would be said: "like a niche within which is a lamp in a glass, as if the glass were a brilliant star," serves to magnify their status and elevate their position, by explanation after vagueness and detail after generality, and by affirming what follows them of them through the mode of predication, which reveals the principal intention, rather than through a descriptive form that indicates mere general establishment. The point is evident. The first sentence has the place of nominative as a description of "lamp," and the second sentence has the place of genitive as a description of "glass." The lam (the particle of attribution) substitutes for the relative pronoun link, as if it were said: "within it is a lamp which is in a glass which is as if it were a brilliant star."

﴿It is lit from a blessed tree﴾ that is, the lighting of the lamp begins from a blessed tree, ﴿blessed﴾, that is, abundant in benefits, in that its wick is fed by its oil. It is said that it is described as blessed only because it grows in the land which Allah, may He be exalted, has blessed for the worlds.

﴿an olive tree﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "tree." The vagueness of it, its description with blessing, and then its substitution, serve to magnify its status. It has been recited as "tuwaqqadu" with a ta, the pronoun standing in place of the subject referring to the glass rather than the lamp. It has also been recited as "tawaqqada" in the past tense of the tafa''ul form, meaning that the beginning of the burning of the lamp is from it. And it has been recited as "tawaqqadu" with one of the two tas deleted, from "tatawaqqadu," with its attribution to the glass.

﴿neither of the east nor of the west﴾: the sun does not fall upon it at one time and not at another, but rather it is situated such that the sun falls upon it throughout the day, unlike one that is on a hill or in an open desert, where the sun falls upon it at sunrise and sunset. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: it is neither exclusively eastern nor exclusively western, but rather both eastern and western; that is, the sun reaches it at its rising and at its setting, so it is both eastern and western, taking its share of both, so its oil is brighter. It is also said: it is not situated at the eastern edge of the inhabited world nor at its western edge, but in its middle, which is the Levant (al-Sham), for its oils are at their finest. It is also said: it is neither in a place (madha) where the sun shines upon it constantly and burns it, nor in a place (maqna'ah) from which the sun is constantly absent and leaves it raw. In a hadith it is said: "There is no good in a tree or a plant in a maqna'ah, and there is no good in either of them in a madha."

﴿its oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it﴾ that is, it is so pure and luminous that it almost shines by itself, without any fire touching it at all. The word "law" (lau, if/even if) in such contexts is not used to indicate the negation of something in the past because of the negation of something else in it, so there is no consequent for it to be considered, which has been omitted with confidence in the indication of the preceding clause upon it, in a deliberate consideration, except when intending to explain the grammatical analysis according to the technical rules of grammar. Rather, it serves to indicate the realization of what the preceding statement implies of the affirmed or negated ruling in every hypothetical state of the states accompanying it, in summary, by placing it upon the most remote of them, either because of the presence of an impediment, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you should be in towers built up high﴾; or because of the absence of a condition, as in this noble verse, so that by its realization or non-realization with it, its realization or non-realization with all other states becomes manifest by way of priority. This is because whenever a thing is realized despite what contradicts it, such as the presence of an impediment or the absence of a condition, then its realization without that is more fitting. For this reason nothing else from among the other states is mentioned with it, and it suffices with the mention of the coordinating wa (and) joining the clause to its counterpart which is opposed to it and which encompasses all states that differ from it when they are multiple. This is what is meant by their saying that it is for the comprehensive enumeration of states in a summary manner. This is a consistent matter in affirmative and negative statements. For when you say: "So-and-so is generous; he gives even if he is poor," or "So-and-so is stingy; he does not give even if he is rich," you intend to show the realization of giving in the first and its non-realization in the second in all supposed states. The implied meaning is: he gives if he were not poor, and even if he were poor; and he does not give if he were not rich, and even if he were rich. So the clause, together with what is conjoined to it, is in the accusative position of a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun implicit in the affirmative or negative verb, that is: he gives, initially giving, being in all states. The implied meaning of the noble verse is: "its oil would almost glow if fire touched it, and even if fire did not touch it," that is, it glows in every state of the presence or absence of the condition. The first clause has been omitted, as is consistent in this matter, because the second clearly indicates it.

﴿Light upon light﴾: "Light" is the predicate of an omitted subject. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿upon light﴾ is related to an omitted element which is a description of it, confirming what the indefiniteness conveys of grandeur. The sentence is a summary (fadhlakah) of the parable and an explicit statement of what resulted from it, and a preparation for what follows. That is: that light by which the Qur'an was expressed, and whose wondrous attribute was represented by what has been detailed of the description of the niche, is a great light existing upon a light like it. It is not that it is an expression for a specific light, or an unspecified light above another light like it, nor for the combination of just two lights, but rather for a light multiplied without limitation as to its multiplication by a specific bound. The specification of the degrees of multiplication of what has been likened, the light of the niche, by what has been mentioned is because it is the furthest degree of its multiplication customarily. For a lamp when it is in a confined place like a niche is brighter for it and more gathering of its light, because of the joining of the reflected ray with the original ray, unlike a spacious place where the light disperses and spreads. The lamp-stand is the most helpful thing for increasing illumination, and likewise the purity of its glass. Beyond these degrees there is nothing that customarily increases its radiance or supplies it with illumination in another degree. Moreover, making "light" an expression for the light being likened is not befitting the dignity of this Glorious Revelation.

﴿Allah guides to His light﴾ that is, He guides with a special guidance that conclusively leads to the sought goal, to that multiplied, greatly significant light. The expression of it in the place of the pronoun is for increasing its affirmation and confirming its inherent grandeur through its grandeur by relation, arising from its being attributed to His pronoun, may He be mighty and majestic. ﴿Whomever He wills﴾ of His servants, by enabling them to understand what it contains of proofs of its truth, of its being from Allah, may He be exalted, such as its inimitability, its reports of the unseen, and other things that necessitate belief in it. In this there is an indication that the basis and foundation of this guidance is nothing but His will, may He be exalted, and that the convergence of causes without it is far from leading to the aims.

﴿And Allah sets forth parables for people﴾ within the course of guidance, as their condition requires, for it has a great role in the domain of guidance. This is because it is the presentation of the intelligible in the form of the sensible, and the depiction of elusive meanings in the form of the familiar. For this reason His light, which is expressed by the Qur'an that clarifies, has been likened to the light of the niche. And the manifestation of the Glorious Name in the place of the pronoun indicates the difference of the state of what is attributed to Him, may He be exalted, of the special guidance and the setting forth of parables, which is of the kind of general guidance, as is made clear by the attachment of the first to "whomever He wills" and the second to "people" in their entirety.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾, whether it be an object or a subject, manifest or hidden. It follows from this that His will is connected with guiding those who are fit for it and deserving of it among people, and not others, since the contrary would contradict the wisdom upon which creation and legislation are founded; and that His general guidance be of various kinds and diverse methods according to what their conditions require. The sentence is a parenthetical concluding clause (i'tiradh tadhyili), confirming what precedes it. The manifestation of the Glorious Name serves to confirm the independence of the sentence and to indicate the cause of the ruling, and the difference in the state of the one ruled upon, in essence and in relation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 36:

﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned﴾. When He mentioned the matter of the noble Qur'an in its explanation of the laws and rulings, their foundations and their ends, along with the reward and punishment that follow from them, and other matters of the Hereafter and its terrors, and when it was indicated that it is in the utmost degree of clarification and manifestation, being likened to the light of the niche, as detailed, and it was indicated that this light, despite being at the highest degree of manifestness, is only followed by one whom Allah the Exalted has willed to guide, and not by anyone else, He followed this with a mention of the two groups and a depiction of some of their deeds that express the state of their guidance or lack thereof. By "houses" is meant all the mosques, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It was also said: they are the mosques built by a prophet of the prophets of Allah the Exalted: the Ka'bah, which was built by Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, the Bayt al-Maqdis, which was built by Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, and the Mosque of Madinah and the Mosque of Quba', which were built by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Its being indefinite (nakirah) is for glorification. By "permission" regarding its raising is meant the command to build it elevated, unlike other houses. It was also said: it is the command to raise its status by worshipping Allah the Exalted in it, so the mention of remembrance following it is in the manner of explanatory conjunction (al-'atf al-tafsiri). In any case, the expression of it as "permission" alludes to the fact that it is fitting for the state of one commanded that he should be oriented toward the commanded matter before its command arrives, intending to fulfil it, as if he were seeking permission for it, so that the command concerning it falls in the place of permission for it. By the mention of His name is meant whatever encompasses all of His remembrances, the Exalted. The word "fi" (in) is connected to the statement of the Exalted: ﴿Glorify Him﴾.

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿in them﴾ is a repetition of it for emphasis and reminder, because of the separation between them, and to signal that the fronting (of the prepositional phrase) is for emphasis, not to restrict glorification to occurring in houses only. The original meaning of tasbih (glorification) is tanzih (declaring transcendence) and taqdis (sanctification). It is used with the lam and without it as well, as in the Exalted's statement: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾. They said: what is meant by it is the obligatory prayers, as is indicated by the specification of the times in the Exalted's statement: ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾, meaning in the mornings (al-ghadawat) and the evenings (al-'ashiyyat). The word "al-ghuduw" is either the plural of "ghadah" like "qunan" as the plural of "qanah," as has been said, or a verbal noun used for the time, as suggested by its being paired with "al-asal." "Al-asal" is the plural of "asil," which is the late afternoon. This includes all the times except the Fajr prayer performed in the morning. It is also permissible that what is meant by it is the act of declaring transcendence itself, on the basis that it is an expression for what occurs during the prayers and their times, for the increase of its honour and preeminence over its other instances, or an expression for what occurs at all times. The singling out of the two ends of the day for mention is because they stand in for all of it, being the principal part of it, by virtue of their being witnessed and by virtue of being the times most commonly associated with the direct undertaking of deeds and the occupation with affairs. It was also read: "wa al-'isal," which means entering the time of asil.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 37:

(p-179) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿men﴾ is the subject (fa'il) of "yusabbihu" (glorify). Its being placed after the adverbial phrases is due to what has passed many times: the concern with what is placed first and the building of suspense toward what is placed last; and also because describing it at length would, if placed first, disrupt the goodness of the arrangement. It has been read as "yusabbihu" in the passive voice, with it ascribed to one of the adverbial phrases, and "rijalun" (men) is nominative by what the narration of the verb indicates without naming the agent, in the manner of his saying:

Labbayka Yazidu, a suppliant for a dispute...

As if it were said: "Who glorifies Him?" and it was answered: "Men glorify Him." It has also been read as "tusabbihu" with the verb feminine and active, because the broken plural may be treated as feminine; and as passive, with it ascribed to the times of morning and evening through the addition of the preposition ba', so that the times are made to be glorifying while they are themselves glorified in; or it is ascribed to the pronoun of the glorification, meaning: the glorification is glorified for Him, through the figurative usage that permits ascribing it to the two times, just as they explained the reading of Abu Ja'far: "li-yujza qawman" (that He may recompense a people), meaning: that the recompense may be recompensed to a people. Indeed, this is better than that, since there is no explicit object here.

﴿Neither trade nor sale distracts them﴾ is a description of "rijal" (men), emphasising what the indefiniteness conveys of grandeur, and indicating the completeness of their devotion to God, may He be exalted, and their absorption in it. What is related of them is glorification without any diverting factor turning them away or any distraction turning them back, whatever it may be. The mention of trade in particular is because these two are the strongest and most well-known distractions for them, meaning: no kind of trade distracts them.

﴿Nor sale﴾ means: nor any single instance of sales, even if it is of the greatest profit. Its being singled out by mention, though it is included under trade, is to signal its superiority over the other kinds of trade, because its profit is certain and immediate, whereas the profit of the others is anticipated in the later state at the time of sale. Therefore, the negation of distraction by other things does not entail the negation of distraction by it. For this reason the word "la" (not) is repeated, to remind of the negation and to emphasise it. It has been reported from al-Waqidi that the meaning of trade is purchasing, because it is its origin and beginning; and it was said: it is bringing in goods, because that is what predominates in it, and from it one says: "tajara fi kadha," meaning he brought it in.

﴿from the remembrance of God﴾ by glorification and praise, ﴿and the establishing of prayer﴾, meaning: establishing it at its appointed times without delay. The ta' that compensates for the dropped middle radical has been omitted through the morphological alteration, and the genitive construction (idafa) has been substituted for it, as in his saying:

And they broke with you the promise of the matter which they promised.

Meaning: the promise of the matter.

﴿and the giving of zakat﴾, meaning: the wealth whose giving to the entitled ones has been prescribed. Its mention here, although it is not something done in houses, is because it is a companion that never separates from the establishing of prayer in most contexts, along with what it contains of an indication that the excellent deeds of these people are not confined to what takes place in the mosques. Likewise his saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they fear﴾ etc., for it is a second description of "rijal," or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of ﴿distracts them﴾; and whichever it is, their fear is not restricted to being in the mosques.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿a day﴾ is an object of "yakhafuna" (they fear), not an adverbial phrase of it. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in which hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾ is a description of "yawman" (a day), meaning: they will be agitated and will change within themselves from terror and dread, and will become fixed in their gaze, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the eyes are dazed and the hearts reach the throats﴾. Or their states will change and turn, so the hearts will gain understanding after having been sealed, and the eyes will see after having been blind. Or the hearts will turn between hoping for salvation and fearing destruction, and the eyes will look from whichever direction they are seized and their records are brought to them.

(p-180) [So that Allah may recompense them] is related to an omitted element indicated by the pleasing deeds that were mentioned. The sense is: they persist in what they do, in constant glorification and remembrance, giving zakat, and fearing [Allah], with nothing diverting them from that, so that Allah, Exalted, may recompense them ﴿with the best of what they did﴾. That is, He recompenses the best reward for their deeds, according to what He promised them: for one good deed, ten like it, up to seven hundredfold.

﴿And adds to them of His bounty﴾. That is, He bestows upon them things that were not promised to them in their specific details or measures, and whose modes and quantities did not occur to their minds. Rather, they were promised only in general terms, as in His saying, Exalted: ﴿For those who did good is the best [reward] and more﴾, and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), relating from Him, Mighty and Majestic: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." And [there are] other generous promises, among which is His saying, Exalted: ﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾. For this is a tadhyil (concluding clause) that confirms the increase: a generous promise that He, Exalted, will give them, beyond the recompense of their deeds, goods that no reckoning can contain.

As for the claim that there was no prior promise of increase, even in general terms, and that it did not occur to them in any way, this is refuted by the arrangement of the verse, which places it in the same sequence as the purpose clause. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is an expression for those whose beautiful qualities have been mentioned, as if it were said: "And Allah provides them without reckoning." He placed it in the position of their pronoun in order to draw attention, through what is in the relative clause (al-silah), to the fact that the basis of the mentioned provision lies purely in His will, not in their described deeds. Likewise, the basis of the guidance previously mentioned to His light is His, Exalted, not the outward causes. It also announces that they are among those whom Allah, Exalted, wills to provide for, just as they are among those whom He wills to guide to His light, as indicated by what has been detailed of their good deeds. For all that was mentioned (remembrance, glorification, establishing prayer, giving zakat, fear of the Last Day and its terrors, and hope for reward) is drawn from the Noble, Mighty Qur'an, which is what is meant by the light. Through it, the explanation of the states of those guided by its guidance is completed in the clearest and most manifest way.

It has been said that His saying, Exalted: ﴿"In houses..."﴾ and what follows is part of the parable (tamthil). The word "in" (fi) is related to an omitted element that serves as a description of the niche (mishkah), meaning: existing in houses. It has also been said that it describes the lamp, or the glass, or that it is related to "is kindled." All of these are unbecoming to the dignity of this noble revelation. How could they not be, when what follows His saying, Exalted: ﴿And if fire had not touched it﴾, according to what is correct, or what follows His saying, Exalted: ﴿Light upon light﴾, according to what has been said, up to His saying, Exalted: ﴿of all things He is Knowing﴾, is a statement definitely related to the thing being illustrated (al-mumaththal)? Therefore, inserting it between the parts of the parable, even though it is like separating the tree from its bark with a foreign element, leads to the mention of the state of those who benefit from the parable and are guided to the light of the Noble Qur'an being made a consequence and a condition, while the description of the state of their opposites is intended in itself. Such a thing is not known in human speech, let alone to be attributed to the inimitable speech.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 39:

﴿And those who disbelieve﴾ is conjoined to what its preceding context leads to, as if it were said: those who believed, their deeds (are as described) in state and outcome, and those who disbelieved, ﴿their deeds﴾, that is, their deeds which are among the avenues of righteousness, such as maintaining ties of kinship, freeing captives, providing water to pilgrims, maintaining the Sacred House, relieving the distressed, hospitality to guests, and the like, which, if accompanied by faith, would entail reward, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord is that their deeds are like ashes...﴾, the verse.

﴿Like a mirage﴾ (sarab), which is what is seen in deserts from the shining of the sun upon them at midday, so that one thinks it is water flowing, that is, running. ﴿In a valley (bi-qi'atin)﴾ is connected to an omitted element that serves as a description of sarab, meaning: existing in a qi'ah, which is the flat, level land. It was also said that qi'ah is the plural of qa'in, like jirah being the plural of jar. It was read as bi-qi'at, with an extended ta', like dimat, either as the plural of qi'ah, or because the original form was qi'ah, whose fatha of the 'ayn was lengthened so that an alif was produced from it.

﴿The thirsty one thinks it to be water﴾ is another description of sarab. The restriction of the thinking to the thirsty one, although it includes everyone who sees it, whoever he may be, whether thirsty or sated, is for completing the simile by realizing the sharing of its two parties in the aspect of resemblance, which is the alluring appearance and the comforting end.

﴿Until when he comes to it﴾, that is, when the thirsty one comes to what he thought was water. It was also said: to its location.

﴿He finds it not﴾, that is, what he thought was water, and on which he had set his hope, ﴿anything﴾, neither a real root nor an imagined one, as he used to see it before, let alone finding water in it. With this, the explanation of the states of the disbelievers is complete by way of simile.

As for His Exalted saying: ﴿And he finds God with him, so He pays him his account in full, and God is swift in reckoning﴾, it is an explanation of the remaining states that befall them after that, by way of completion, lest it be imagined that the utmost of their condition is only disappointment and despair, as is the case of the thirsty one. It appears that after that simile there befalls them the non-finding of their mentioned deeds, neither as a substance nor as a trace, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾. How not, since the ruling that the deeds of the disbelievers are like a mirage which the thirsty one thinks is water, until when he comes to it he finds it nothing, is a ruling that they are such that they think them beneficial for them in the Hereafter, until when they come to them they find them nothing. As if it were said: until when the disbelievers come on the Day of Resurrection to their deeds which they used to think beneficial for them in the Hereafter, they find them nothing, and they find God, that is, His judgment and decree, at the time of arrival. It was also said: at the time of the deed. So He pays them in full, that is, He gives them their account completely, that is, the account of their mentioned deeds and their recompense, for their belief in their benefit without faith, and their acting upon that, is disbelief upon their disbelief, which necessarily merits punishment. The singularity of the two pronouns referring to ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ is either for intending the genus, like the singular noun in the simile, or for taking each one of them individually; likewise the singularity of what refers to their deeds. This is it. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning Utbah ibn Rabi'ah ibn Umayyah, who had been devout in the Jahiliyyah, wore woolen garments, and sought the religion, but when Islam came, he disbelieved.

﴿Or like darkness﴾ is a conjunction with ﴿like a mirage﴾. The word ﴿or﴾ (aw) is used for diversification (tanwi') after the comparison of their deeds, on which they relied most strongly and of which they boasted everywhere, with the state of the mirage mentioned, together with an added reckoning and punishment. Their wicked deeds, in which there is no trace of goodness that the deceived are misled by, are compared to darkness that exists ﴿in a deep sea﴾, that is, deep and abundant in water, attributed to al-lujj (the deep, i.e., the greater part of the sea's water). It is said that it is attributed to al-lujja, which is also the greater part of it.

﴿Covering it﴾ is another qualifier of the sea, meaning it conceals and completely covers it. ﴿A wave﴾. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿above it is a wave﴾, is a clause consisting of a subject and predicate, its place in i'rab being nominative, as a qualifier of ﴿a wave﴾. Or the qualifier is the prepositional phrase, and the second ﴿wave﴾ is its subject, since it relies on the modified noun. The discussion of it is as mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, "light upon light" (24:35), that is: waves piled up and layered upon one another cover it. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿above it is a cloud﴾, is a qualifier of the second ﴿wave﴾ according to one of the two mentioned possibilities, meaning: above that wave is a dark cloud that concealed the light of the stars. In this there is an indication of the extreme degree of the accumulation of the waves and their multiplication, to the point that they seem to have reached the cloud. ﴿Darkness﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: they are darknesses, ﴿some of them above others﴾, that is, densely packed and piled up. This is an explanation of the complete intensity of the darkness, just as His saying, exalted is He, "light upon light" explains the utmost strength of the light, except that the former relates to the compared element (al-mushabbah) and this to the element compared to (al-mushabbah bihi), as what follows it indicates. It was read in the genitive as a substitution (badal) for the first. It was also read with the cloud construed as a genitive construction with it.

﴿When he brings out﴾, that is, the one who is afflicted with them. Its omission without mention is because the meaning clearly indicates it.

﴿his hand﴾: he places it within his sight, close to his eye, so that he looks at it, ﴿he can hardly see it﴾, though it is the nearest thing to him, let alone that he should see it.

﴿And whoever Allah does not give light﴾, etc., is a concluding parenthetical statement (i'tiraḍ tadhyili), brought in to establish what the comparison conveyed, namely that the deeds of the disbelievers are as detailed, and to confirm that this is due to His not guiding them to His light. The relative pronoun is used to indicate, through what is in its clause, the cause of the ruling. Whoever Allah has not willed to guide, that is: whoever Allah has not willed to guide to His light, which is the Qur'an, with a special guidance that necessarily entails being rightly guided, and has not directed toward faith in it.

﴿Then for him there is no light﴾, that is: then for him there is no guidance at all from anyone whatsoever.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen﴾ and so on, is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, to inform him that God, Exalted is He, bestowed upon him ﷺ the highest and most manifest ranks of light, and explained to him the most subtle and most hidden secrets of the dominion (mulk) and the realm of the unseen (malakut). The hamza here is for confirmation (li-l-taqrir), meaning: you have indeed acquired a certain knowledge, resembling direct observation in its strength and firmness, through clear revelation and sound reasoning.

﴿That God glorifies Him﴾, meaning: He exalts Him, Exalted is He, continually, in His essence, His attributes, and His acts, far above everything unbefitting His majestic glory, such as deficiency or defect.

﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: what is in them. This is either by way of their dwelling within them, of rational beings and others, whatever they may be, or by way of their being parts of them, as a glorification that sound minds comprehend. For every existent among the possible existents, whether composite or simple, by its quiddity and by the existence of its states, points to the existence of a Creator who necessarily exists, characterized by the attributes of perfection, sanctified above everything unbefitting any of His majestic affairs. He has drawn attention to the full strength of this indication and the utmost clarity of it, in that He expressed it through what pertains to rational beings, namely glorification (tasbih), which is the strongest and most manifest degree of exaltation, by treating the tongue of state as though it were the tongue of speech. He emphasized this by choosing the word "man" (who) over "ma" (what), as if everything, whether lofty or lowly, and every individual of the accidents and substances, were rational, speaking, and truthfully reporting the exaltedness of His rank and the might of His sovereignty. The specific mention of exaltation, although the things in the heavens and the earth also indicate His being characterized by the attributes of perfection, is because the context of the speech is to condemn the state of those who reflect, in their failing to exalt Him by making inanimate things partners with Him in divinity, and by attributing to Him the taking of offspring, exalted is He far above that by a great exaltation. And to interpret glorification as what befits each kind of created being, by taking it to mean a figurative sense that includes the glorification of rational beings and others, as is apparent from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Each indeed knows its prayer and its glorification﴾, is refuted by the fact that some rational beings, namely the disbelievers among the two groups (humans and jinn), certainly do not glorify Him in that sense. Their glorification is only the indication mentioned, which non-rational beings also share with them. In this there is further rebuke of them and reproach, by showing that they glorify Him in terms of their lowest aspects, which are inanimacy, corporeality, and animality, and not in terms of their highest aspect, which is humanity.

﴿And the birds﴾, in the nominative case, coordinated with "whoever" (man). Their specific mention, although they are included among what is in the earth, is because their resting place is unstable and because of their independence through a skilled craftsmanship and a marvelous creation. Their glorification is intended to be explained from that aspect, due to the clarity of their announcing the perfect power of their Maker and the subtle arrangement of their Originator, as is indicated by the restriction in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿lined up﴾, meaning: their glorification of Him, Exalted is He, while they are spreading their wings. For His giving the heavy bodies the ability to remain in the air and to move as they wish, through wings and light tails, and His guiding them to the manner of using them by folding and spreading, is a shining proof, clear in its hidden meaning, and a manifest sign for people who understand, indicating the perfect power of the skillful Maker and the utmost wisdom of the Originator who restores.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Each indeed knows its prayer and its glorification﴾ is an explanation of the complete firmness of each one of what has been mentioned in exalting Him, and the rootedness of its foot therein, by depicting its state as that of one who knows what proceeds from him of actions, and so does them deliberately and with intention, not by chance without thought. Within this is included an allusion to the fact that each of the things mentioned, together with the exaltation mentioned, has an essential need for Him, Exalted is He, and an overflow from Him for what concerns it, through the tongue of its readiness, and the verification of this is that every one of the possible existents, in itself, is far from deserving existence, but it is ready to have overflowing upon it from Him, Exalted is He, what befits His majesty of existence and what follows it of perfections, at its beginning and its continuance. So it constantly receives an overflow from Him, Exalted is He, so that there is poured upon it at every moment, from the overflowings of the sciences related to His essence and attributes, what the scope of expression cannot encompass, such that if the connection between it and the care and lordship were cut off, it would cease to exist in an instant. This overflow in meaning is expressed by prayer (salat), which is supplication and entreaty, in order to complete the figurative depiction and to convey the qualities mentioned earlier in detail. Its being placed before glorification in the mention is because it precedes it in rank. Moreover, it is permissible that "knows" (alima) be in its literal sense, and that it means absolute perception; and by what the tanwin replaces (i.e., the word "kull" with its tanwin), in every kind and individual of birds, and by the prayer and the glorification is meant what God, Exalted is He, inspired in each one of them, of the specific supplication and glorification peculiar to it. However, this should not be on the basis that the bird is coordinated with the word "man" and raised by its governing particle, for that would lead to the glorification being understood in a figurative sense that includes the speech-glorification and the state-glorification of rational beings and others, and you have known what is wrong with that. Rather, it is by means of a concealed verb, meant to express the glorification specific to birds, coordinated with what was mentioned, as passed in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and many among the people﴾. That is: the birds glorify with a glorification specific to them while they are spreading their wings. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Each indeed knows its prayer and its glorification﴾ means: its supplication and its glorification, which God, mighty and majestic, inspired in it, to show the completeness of its firmness in them, and that their issuing from it is not by chance and without thought, but from knowledge and certainty, without any deficiency in either of them, as God, Exalted is He, inspired. For His inspiring, Exalted is He, each kind of created being with subtle knowledge, which the most astute of rational beings can hardly reach, is something whose denial is not possible at all. How could it not be, when the hedgehog, despite being among the things farthest from perception, is said to sense the north and south winds before they blow, so it changes the entrance to its burrow? It is related that there was in Constantinople before the Islamic conquest a man who had grown rich because he used to warn people of winds before they blew, and they benefited from his warning by preparing for their ships and other matters. The cause of that was that he kept a hedgehog in his house, and by its states one could infer what has been mentioned. The specific mention of the glorification of birds in this meaning is because their voices are more manifest in existence and closer to being understood as glorification.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And God is Knowing of what they do﴾, meaning: of what they do, is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraz) confirming the content of what precedes it. The word "ma" (what), on the first interpretation, refers to the indication mentioned, which encompasses all existents, rational and others, and the expression of it as an act attributed to the pronoun of rational beings is for the reason already mentioned several times. On the second interpretation, it either refers to that indication together with the specific glorification of birds, or to the glorification of birds alone. Then the verb is in its literal sense, and its attribution to the pronoun of rational beings is for the reason mentioned, and the parenthetical clause in that case confirms the glorification of birds alone. On the first two interpretations, it confirms the glorification of all. Furthermore, it has been said that the pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He, "has known" refers to God, mighty and majestic, and the pronoun in ﴿its prayer and its glorification﴾ refers to "each." That is: God, Exalted is He, has known the prayer of each one of what is in the heavens and the earth, and its glorification. Then the parenthetical clause in that case confirms its content in both interpretations, but on the condition that "ma" refers to what His knowledge, Exalted is He, has encompassed of its prayer and glorification, and indeed of all its states that befall it and its acts that proceed from it; and these two are included in it by primary inclusion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 42:

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, not to other than Him, because He is the Creator of them both and of what is in them, of essences and attributes, and He is the One who disposes of all of them, bringing into existence and annihilating, originating and returning.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah﴾, that is, to Him alone, exalted is He, and not to other than Him, ﴿is the final return﴾, that is, the return of all things through annihilation and resurrection. It is an explanation of the exclusivity of dominion to Him, exalted is He, in the return (ma'ad), following the explanation of His exclusivity in the origin (mabda'). The placing of the august Name (Allah) in the position where a pronoun would be expected serves to instill awe and to indicate the cause of the ruling.

﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives along clouds﴾. *Al-izjā'* means moving a thing gently and easily. The word is used mainly for moving something small or insignificant, as in *al-bidā'ah al-muzjāh* ("meagre merchandise"). It therefore implies that the cloud, relative to His power, is something of no account.

﴿then joins them together﴾, i.e., joins its parts together by bringing some of them to others. It was also read *yuwallifu* without a hamza.

﴿then makes it piled up﴾, i.e., heaped one upon another. ﴿So you see the rain﴾, i.e., the rain, emerging as a result of its accumulation and thickening. His saying ﴿coming out from within it﴾, i.e., from its openings, is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) relating to *al-wadq* (the rain), because the seeing is visual. The mention of seeing it coming out, following the mention of the making, rather than its simply coming out, expresses hyperbole about the speed of its emergence, in the manner of His saying, "So We said: Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted" (2:60; 26:63). It also shows the care taken to establish the seeing, which is obvious. *Khilāl* is the plural of *khalal*, like *jibāl* of *jabal*. It was also said to be a singular, like *ḥijāb* and *ḥijāz*, and what supports this is that it was read *min khalalihi*.

﴿And He sends down from the sky﴾, i.e., from the clouds, since everything above you is sky, ﴿mountains﴾, i.e., masses of bulk resembling mountains in size, ﴿within it﴾. His saying ﴿of hail﴾ is the object of *yunazzilu* on the basis that *min* is partitive (*tab'īḍiyyah*), while the first two instances of *min* indicate the starting point (*ibtidā' al-ghāyah*). On this view the second *min* is an inclusive apposition (*badal al-ishtimāl*) from the first, with the preposition repeated. The meaning is: He sends down, starting from the sky, from mountains within it, some hail that strikes. It was also said that the object is elided and that *min barad* is an explanation (*bayān*) of *al-jibāl*, meaning: He sends down, starting from the sky, from mountains within it of the same kind as hail, as hail. The first view is more evident, because it avoids assuming an elision and specifying part of what is sent down. It was also said that the object is ﴿mountains﴾ on the basis that *min* is partitive, and ﴿of hail﴾ is an explanation of *al-jibāl*, meaning: He sends down from the sky some mountains that are within it, of hail, that is, likened to mountains in abundance. In any case, the fronting of the prepositional phrase before the object is, as has been noted more than once, for the sake of giving attention to what is fronted and creating suspense for what is delayed. (p-185) It was also said that by "the sky" is meant the canopy, and that within it are mountains of hail, just as in the earth there are mountains of stone, and nothing in reason rules this out by any decisive proof. The well-known view is that when vapours rise and are not dissolved by heat, they reach the cold layer of the air, and when the cold intensifies they gather there and become cloud. If the cold does not intensify, they fall as rain in drops. If it intensifies, then if it reaches the vapour particles before they gather, it falls as snow, and otherwise as hail. Sometimes the air becomes excessively cold, so it contracts and condenses into cloud, from which rain or snow falls. All of this is attributed to the governance of Allah, the Exalted, and to His will, which is based on wisdom and benefits.

﴿He afflicts with it﴾, i.e., with what He sends down of hail, ﴿whom He wills﴾, by afflicting him with it, so that he suffers what harm he suffers to his person and property.

﴿And averts it from whom He wills﴾, by turning it away from him, so that he is saved from its harm. ﴿The brilliance of its lightning nearly﴾, i.e., the light of the lightning of the cloud described with what has preceded of driving, joining and so on. The attribution of the lightning to the cloud before the statement of its existence in it serves to announce that its matter is manifest and needs no explicit mention. It was read with *al-madd* (elongation), meaning elevation and height; with the assimilation of the *dāl* into the *sīn*; and *burqahu* with a fatḥah on the *rā'*, as the plural of *burqah*, which is an amount of lightning, like *ghurfah*; and with a ḍammah on it, to match the ḍammah of the *bā'*.

﴿Takes away the sight﴾, i.e., snatches it because of the excess of the illumination and the speed of its arrival. The unrestricted mention of "the sights" adds to the awe of its matter and shows how strongly it affects them, as if it nearly takes them away even when they are closed. This is among the strongest proofs of the perfection of power, since it produces opposite from opposite. It was read *yudhhibu* from *al-idhhāb* with the extra *bā'*.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 44:

﴿God turns the night and the day﴾ by the alternation of the two, or by the decrease of one and the increase of the other, or by changing their conditions through heat and cold and other things that occur within them, among which is what has been mentioned of the driving of the clouds and what results from it.

﴿Indeed in that﴾ is a reference to what was detailed just before, and the sense of distance in it, despite the closeness of what is referred to, serves to announce the elevation of its rank after its station.

﴿is a lesson﴾ meaning: a clear proof of the existence of the Eternal Creator, His oneness, the perfection of His power, the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all things, the efficacy of His will, and His transcendence above whatever is unbefitting the dignity of the Most High.

﴿for those endowed with sight﴾ for everyone who has sight.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 45:

﴿And Allah created every moving creature﴾ That is: every living being that crawls upon the earth. It is also read "Khaliqu kulli dabbah" (the Creator of every moving creature), in the genitive construction.

﴿from water﴾ which is a part of its substance, or a specific water, namely the sperm-drop (nutfah). In that case it is the mention of the predominant as if it were the whole, since among living beings there are some that come into being not from a sperm-drop. It has also been said that "from water" is connected to "moving creature" and is not the complement of "created."

﴿Of them is one that goes upon its belly﴾ like the serpent. Calling its movement "walking" although it is crawling is by way of metaphor (isti'arah) or by mushakalah (analogy of wording).

﴿And of them is one that walks upon two legs﴾ like humans and birds, ﴿and of them is one that walks upon four﴾ like livestock and wild animals. The creatures that walk on more than four, such as spiders and similar insects, are not mentioned because they are not taken into account. The pronoun in "minhum" is masculine to give precedence to rational beings (taghlib al-'uqala'), and the expression of the categories with the word "man" (who) is so that the detail corresponds to the summary. The order is for placing first what is more evident as a manifestation of power.

﴿Allah creates what He wills﴾ of what has been mentioned and what has not been mentioned, whether simple or compound, in whatever forms, limbs, shapes, movements, natures, faculties and actions He wills, while the element is one. The explicit use of the noble Name in place of the pronoun is to magnify the matter of the creation mentioned and to indicate that it is among the requirements of divinity.

﴿Indeed Allah is over all things Competent﴾ so He does what He wills as He wills. The explicit mention of the Majesty for what has been mentioned, together with the emphasis on the independence of the explanatory resumption (isti'naf ta'lili).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 46:

﴿Indeed, We have sent down clear signs⁠﴾ i.e., for everything whose clarification is fitting, of the religious rulings (aḥkām) and the cosmic mysteries (asrār takwīniyya).

﴿And Allah guides whom He wills⁠﴾ to guide him, by His enabling (tawfīq) him to look correctly into them and by directing him to reflect upon their inner meanings, ﴿to a straight path⁠﴾ that leads to the reality of the Truth and to success in Paradise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 47:

﴿They say: "We believe in Allah and in the Messenger"﴾ This begins the explanation of the states of some of those whom Allah did not will to guide to the Straight Path. Al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites who would display faith and conceal disbelief. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Bishr the hypocrite, who disputed with a Jew. The Jew called him to the Prophet ﷺ, but he called the Jew to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. It was also said: it was revealed concerning al-Mughirah ibn Wa'il, who disputed with 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) over land and water, and refused to be judged by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Whatever the case, the plural form is used to indicate that the speaker has a group who support and back him in that statement, just as it is said: "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," when the killer is only one of them.

﴿And we obey﴾ That is, we obey it (Allah and the Messenger) in what is commanded and what is forbidden. ﴿Then a faction of them turns away﴾ from accepting its judgment ﴿after that﴾ That is, after what has proceeded from them of claiming faith in Allah and the Messenger and obedience to them both in detail. The sense of distance in "after that" indicates that this is a matter of great weight that must be observed.

﴿And those are not﴾ This is a reference to the speakers, not only to the faction among them who turn away, because denying faith from the speakers does not require denying it from the first group, unlike the reverse; for denying it from the speakers necessarily entails denying it from them in the most emphatic and forceful way. The sense of distance in "those" indicates the remoteness of their rank in disbelief and corruption. That is: those who claim faith and obedience, then some of them turn away, who share with them in the pact and the action, are ﴿not among the believers﴾ That is, not truly believers, as the preposition (lam) indicates; that is, they are not the believers known for sincerity in faith and steadfastness upon it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 48:**

﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them﴾, i.e., the Messenger, ﴿between them﴾, because he is the one who directly executes the judgment in reality, even though that judgment is in reality the judgment of Allah. The mention of Allah the Exalted here serves to magnify him (ﷺ) and to announce the greatness of his station with Him, Exalted is He.

﴿Then a party of them turn away﴾, i.e., a party of them suddenly turned away from being brought to judgment before him (ﷺ), because the right was against them, namely that he (ﷺ) would judge in accordance with the truth against them. This is an explanation of "turning away" (tawalli) and an intensification of it.

**﴿And if the truth is theirs﴾** not against them, **﴿they come to him willingly﴾** submitting, **﴿obedient﴾**, because they are certain that he will judge in their favor. The "ilā" (إلى) is a *ṣilah* (a complementary particle attached to the verb) of *layya'tū* (ليأتوا). The verbs *al-ityān* (الإتيان, "coming") and *al-majī'* (المجيء, "arriving") take "ilā" as their complement, or the word *mudh'inīn* (مُذْعِنِين) is connected with "ilā" through *tadmīn* (التضمين, "implicit meaning," where one word is given the sense of another), with the sense of hastening and approaching, as in God's words: ﴿So they came hastening to him﴾. The fronting (*al-taqdīm*, التقديم) is for exclusivity.

﴿Is there a disease in their hearts?﴾ This is a denial and a condemnation of their aversion mentioned above, and an explanation of its source, after enumerating a number of established vices in them and expected from them, and after considering the various possible sources among them. Therefore the focus of the interrogation is not the thing directly governed by the interrogative particle (the hamza). Rather, it is one of the three matters, or more precisely, its being the source of that aversion. It is as if it were said: "Is that, i.e., their aversion mentioned above, because they are people with diseased hearts, due to their disbelief and hypocrisy?"

﴿Or﴾ because ﴿they have doubts﴾ about the matter of his prophethood (ﷺ) even though its truth is manifest, ﴿or﴾ because ﴿they fear that God and His Messenger will wrong them﴾.

Then he turned away from all of these, nullified the claim that this is their source, and ruled that the source is something else among their abominable acts, when it was said: ﴿Rather, they are the wrongdoers﴾. That is: it is not due to any of the things mentioned. As for the first two, if it were due to any of them, they would have turned away from him (ﷺ) when the truth was in their favour, and they would not have come to him (ﷺ) submitting to his judgment, since their hypocrisy and doubt would also have been established at that time. As for the third, it is entirely absent, since they did not fear any injustice at all, given their knowledge of the details of his (ﷺ) circumstances in trustworthiness and steadfastness upon the truth. Rather, it is because they are the wrongdoers: they want to wrong the one who has a right over them, and they want their denial of it to succeed, so they refuse to be brought to judgment before him (ﷺ), knowing that he (ﷺ) will judge against them in accordance with the truth. Thus, the negation derived from the turning away (idrab) in the first two cases concerns only the attribute of their being the source of the aversion, while their existence in themselves is established. In the third, the negation concerns both the root and the attribute together.

This being said, doubt has been specified as having a cause that makes its occurrence among them possible in general. The meaning is: or they doubted because they saw from him (ﷺ) an accusation, and their trust and certainty in him (ﷺ) departed. In that case, the negation concerns both the doubt itself and its being the source. So reflect carefully on what has been mentioned in detail, and set aside what has been said otherwise.

It was said, as the sound reasoning requires: ﴿The saying of the believers was only﴾ with the accusative (naṣb), on the basis that it is the predicate (khabar) of *kāna* (was), and *anna* together with what follows it in its scope is its subject (ism). It was also read with the nominative (raf'), in reverse. The first reading is stronger in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis), because for the nominal sentence the better choice as subject is the item that is more definite. That is the verb introduced by *an* (that), since there is no way to make it indefinite. By contrast, "the saying of the believers" admits indefiniteness, as when the annexation (iḍāfa) is removed from it. However, the reading with the nominative is more solid in terms of meaning and more fitting to the requirements of the context, because the point of the benefit and the place of clarification in sentences is the predicate. So the more deserving of being the predicate is what conveys more information and more clearly indicates occurrence (ḥudūth), and what contains specific relations that are far from occurring in external reality and in the hearer's mind. There is no doubt that this is more complete and perfect here in *anna* together with what follows it. Thus it is more deserving of being the predicate. As for what the annexation conveys of the general, unspecified relation of the saying, since it is of little use and easy to attain both externally and mentally, its proper treatment is to be considered in a general way and made a heading for the subject. So the meaning is: the saying of the believers, in general, whenever ﴿they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge﴾, that is, the Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿between them﴾, that is, between them and their adversaries, whether those are of their own kind or others, ﴿is only that they say: "We hear and we obey"﴾. That is, the specific nature of this saying reported about them, not any other saying at all.
