As for the reading with the accusative, its meaning is: the saying of the believers was only, that is, it was only their saying at the call, the specific saying reported about them. In it there is, by making the more specific of the two relations and the more remote from occurrence and presence in minds, and the more deserving of clarification, established as a given and made the heading for the subject, while bringing forth what is contrary to it in the position of primary intention, what is not hidden. It was also read: "that he may judge" (*liyuḥkama*) with the verb built for the passive, with its verbal noun (maṣdar) as its subject, corresponding to His saying, "when they are called." That is: that judgment may be carried out, as in His saying, ﴿There has been severed between you﴾, that is, severance has occurred between you.

﴿And those﴾ is a reference to the believers in consideration of the utterance of the aforementioned saying from them. The sense of distance in it is to indicate the elevation of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence. That is: those who are described by what was mentioned of the beautiful description, ﴿they are the successful﴾, that is, they are the ones who attain every aim and the ones who are saved from every harm.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 52:

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), brought to affirm the content of what precedes it regarding the good state of the believers, and to encourage others to join their ranks. That is: and whoever obeys them both, whoever he may be, in what they have been commanded of the legislated rulings, both those that are obligatory and those that are transitive (muta'addiyah). It has been said: in the obligations and the recommended practices (sunan). The first is more suitable to the context.

﴿and fears Allah and keeps his duty to Him﴾ with the qaf sukun (i.e., the qaf pronounced with sukun), which is built upon its being likened to kitf (shoulder). It is also read with the qaf and the ha' pronounced with kasra, and with the ha' pronounced with sukun. That is: and fears Allah for what has passed of his sins, and keeps his duty to Him regarding what lies ahead.

﴿Then those﴾ — those described by what has been mentioned of obedience, fear, and taqwa — ﴿they are the victorious﴾ through everlasting bliss, not those other than them.

**And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths.** This is a report of another of their lies, confirmed with false oaths (*al-aymān al-fājira*). His words, exalted is He, **"with their most emphatic oaths"** (*jahda aymānihim*), are in the accusative because it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) emphasizing its verb, which is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to the subject of "they swore." The meaning is: they swore by Him, exalted is He, striving in their oaths with great effort. The sense of *jahd al-yamīn* is reaching its utmost limit, by way of metaphor (*istiʿāra*), from the expression "he exerted himself" (*jahida nafsahu*) when he reached the full extent of his capacity and strength. That is, they were striving and reaching the highest degrees of oath in intensity and firmness. It was also said that it is a verbal noun emphasizing "they swore," meaning they swore an oath made with exertion. Muqatil said: "Whoever swears by God has exerted himself in the oath."

**"If you order them,"** that is, to go out to fight, not out of their homes and their wealth, as has been said, because this is a report of what they used to say to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Wherever you are, we will be with you; if you go out, we will go out; if you stay, we will stay; and if you order us to fight, we will fight." His words, exalted is He, **"they will surely go out"** (*layakhrujunna*), are the answer to "they swore," by way of reporting their action and not reporting their statement. Since their speech was false and their oath was wicked, He commanded him (ﷺ) to reject it, saying: **"Say"** (*qul*), that is, as a rebuttal to them and a rebuke against them for uttering it, and to show that it is not accepted because they are lying in it, **"Do not swear"** (*lā tuqsimū*), that is, regarding what your speech indicates of obedience.

His words, exalted is He, **"reasonable obedience"** (*ṭāʿatun maʿrūfa*), are the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a justification for the prohibition. That is: do not swear about what you claim of obedience, because your obedience is hypocritical obedience, existing only with the tongue without agreement from the heart. He expressed it as "known" (*maʿrūfa*) only to announce that its being so is famous and known to everyone. It was also read in the accusative, and the meaning would be: you obey with a known obedience. Furthermore, to interpret it as true obedience by supplying something suitable of a subject, predicate, or verb, like "what is demanded of you is true reasonable obedience, not hypocritical," or "reasonable obedience that is better," or "let it be reasonable obedience," or "obey with reasonable obedience," is something the context does not support.

**"Indeed God is Aware of what you do"** (*inna Allāha khabīrun bimā taʿmalūn*), of the actions, both outward and inward, among which are what you show of lies confirmed with wicked oaths, and what you conceal in your hearts of disbelief, hypocrisy, the resolve to deceive the believers, and other kinds of evil and corruption. The sentence is a justification for the ruling that their obedience is hypocritical obedience, which indicates that the basis of the fame of this matter among the believers is His, exalted is He, informing them of that, and a warning to them that He will repay them for all their evil deeds, among which is their hypocrisy.

(p-189)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 54:

﴿Say: "Obey Allah, and obey the Messenger."﴾ The command to "say" is repeated to show the utmost care for this matter, and to signal that the two commands differ. What is said in the first is a prohibition, in the manner of rejection and rebuke, as in His saying, ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾. What is said in the second is a command, in the manner of obligation and legislation. The obedience commanded is stated without qualifiers such as "sound" or "sincere" or the like, after their obedience was described with what was mentioned, to alert that it is not obedience at all.

As for His saying, ﴿But if they turn away﴾, it is addressed to those commanded to obey by Him, the Exalted. It comes to emphasize the command to obey, to intensify the obligation to comply with it, and to drive compliance through warning and encouragement. This is because changing a discourse that is directed toward one meaning, and diverting it from its established course, indicates a new concern on the part of the speaker with the matter, and draws greater desire for it from the listener, as has been pointed out in the explanation of His saying, ﴿Even if We brought the like of it as a supplement﴾. This is especially so when the change is from address through an intermediary to direct address, for His addressing them directly after commanding them through the mediation of the Prophet (ﷺ), and His taking up the explanation of the ruling on compliance with the command and on turning away from it, both in general and in detail, conveys an emphasis and intensity beyond which there is nothing. To suppose that this falls under the "saying" that was commanded to be conveyed from Him, the Exalted, and that it is more forceful in rebuke, is to reverse the matter.

The "fa" (then) indicates that what follows is consequent upon the Prophet's (ﷺ) conveying of what he was commanded to convey to them. Its not being stated explicitly signals the extreme clarity of his (ﷺ) hastening to convey what he was commanded, and that mention of it is unnecessary. That is: if you turn away from obedience after you were commanded to it, ﴿then upon him is﴾, meaning: know that upon him (ﷺ) is ﴿only what he has been charged with﴾, meaning what he was commanded to convey, which you have witnessed at His saying, ﴿Obey Allah, and obey the Messenger.﴾

﴿And upon you is what you have been charged with﴾, meaning what you were commanded to do of obedience. Perhaps the expression of it as "being charged" (tahmil) is to indicate its weight and that it is a burden that remains upon them afterward, as if it were said: when you have turned away from that, you remain under that heavy load. His saying, ﴿what he has been charged with﴾, is to be understood as a case of al-mushakalah (matching of terms, a rhetorical device in which one word is used for another because of their association).

﴿And if you obey him﴾, meaning in what he has commanded you of obedience, ﴿you will be guided﴾ to the truth, which is the ultimate aim that leads to every good and saves from every evil. Its placement after the statement of the ruling on turning away is because putting warning first makes the encouragement stronger and brings it closer to what is of its kind, namely the gracious promise.

His saying, ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD) that confirms what precedes it, namely that the harm of turning away and the benefit of obedience are confined to them. The definite article in "al-Rasul" may be for the genus, which includes him (ﷺ) (p-190) in a primary way, or for a specific reference. That is: upon the kind of Messenger, whoever he may be, is only the conveyance; or upon him (ﷺ) is only the conveyance that makes clear everything that needs clarification, or "al-mubin" is the clear one, taking "mubin" from abana in the sense of baana (to be clear). You know that he has already done this in a way that leaves nothing more to be added, and what remains is only ﴿what you have been charged with﴾.

Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on Surah 24, verse 55:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah has promised those of you who believe﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a new sentence that restates what came before) which confirms the noble promise in His saying, ﴿and if you obey him, you will be guided﴾. It expresses that promise explicitly and specifies the details of the various religious and worldly felicities that were summarised there, which are among the fruits of being guided. It also includes what is meant by the obedience on which guidance was made dependent. By "those who believe" is meant everyone who is characterised by faith after disbelief, absolutely, from whatever group and at whatever time. It does not mean only those of the hypocrites who believed, nor only those who believed after the revelation of this noble verse. The necessity of the general scope of the noble promise, to all without exception, requires this. Thus the address in "of you" is to the general body of disbelievers, not to the hypocrites specifically, and "of" (*min*) is partitive (*tab'idiyyah*).

﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with "believe" and falls within the same scope of the relative clause (*sila*). By it the obedience that was commanded, and on which what is arranged in the course of the noble promise was made to depend, is completed in its explanation, as has been indicated. The placing of the adverbial phrase ("of you") between the two conjoined verbs serves to show the originality and nobility of faith in bringing about its effects and rulings, and to indicate that it is the first thing demanded of them and the most important duty upon them. As for its being postponed after them both in His saying: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds among them forgiveness and a great reward﴾, this is because "of" (*min*) there is explanatory (*bayaniyyah*), and the referent of the pronoun is "those who are with him" (ﷺ), who are the sincere believers. There is no doubt that they combine faith with righteous deeds and persist in both. Therefore their explanation must come after mention of their sublime attributes in their full perfection.

Moreover, whoever makes the address to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the community in general, taking "of" as partitive, and makes the first part (addressed to the Prophet ﷺ) and those with him among the believers in particular, taking "of" as explanatory, has departed far from what the coherence (*siba*) and context (*siyaq*) of the noble composition require, and has strayed far, by many stages, from what befits his station (ﷺ).

﴿He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ is the answer to the oath (*qasam*), either by implication, or by treating His promise as if it were an oath, because its fulfilment is certain without doubt. That is: He will make them successors who dispose of it as kings dispose of their realms, or a succession of those who were not in their state of faith and righteous deeds.

﴿as He made successors those who were before them﴾: these are the Children of Israel, whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made successors in Egypt and Syria after He destroyed Pharaoh and the tyrants. Or it means they and those nations before them who were believers, to whom He pointed in His saying: ﴿Has there not come to you the report of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, none knows them but Allah? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs…﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Then their Lord revealed to them: We will surely destroy the wrongdoers﴾ ﴿and We will surely settle you in the land after them…﴾. The place of the *kaf* (in *kama*, "as") is in the accusative, being a similative infinitive (*masdar tashbihi*) emphasising the verb after it, which has already been emphasised by the oath. The *ma* is verbal (*masdariyyah*). That is: He will surely make them successors in a manner like His making successors those who were before them.

It is also read *kamaustukhlifa* (passive voice). In that case the operative element for the *kaf* is not the verb mentioned, but what it indicates, namely a passive verb which takes the place of a reflexive-like verb (*mutawa'ah*). For His making them successors necessarily entails that they are made successors. It is as if it were said: He will make them successors in the earth, and they will be made successors in it, in a manner of being made successors; that is, a state of being made successors like the state of those before them. Its verification has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿as Moses was asked before﴾. Of this kind is His saying: ﴿and made it grow a good growth﴾, according to one of the two interpretations, meaning: so it grew a good growth. To this is also the saying of one who said:

*A bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of wealth nothing but the stripped-bare and the shorn.*

That is: there remained only the stripped-bare, and so on.

﴿and He will surely establish for them their religion﴾ is coordinated with "He will surely make them successors", forming part of the same answer to the oath. Its being postponed after it, although it is the most sublime of the desired promised things and the greatest of them, is because souls incline more to immediate benefits. So beginning the promises with them is more effective in winning hearts. The meaning is: He will surely make their religion firm and established, such that they continue to act upon its rulings and refer to it in everything they do and leave undone. The expression of this by "establishment" (*tamkin*), which is making one thing a place for another, is said: "He established for him in the land", that is, He made it a dwelling-place for him. Of this is His saying: ﴿We established him in the land﴾ and similar. The word "in" (*fi*) indicates that what is made a dwelling for them is a portion of the land, not all of it, to show the perfect stability of the religion, the solidity of its rulings, and its safety from alteration and change. This is because it is founded on the comparison of it to the earth in stability and firmness, along with what it contains of observing the correspondence between it and the successorship in the earth. The placing of the complement of "establish" before its direct object is for haste in explaining that what is promised is among their benefits, to excite their desire for it and to encourage them to accept it when it comes. Also, placing it between it and its descriptive clause, namely His saying: ﴿which He has approved for them﴾, and postponing it after that, both involve a disturbance of the noble composition's eloquence, which is not hidden. In attributing the religion to them, which is the religion of Islam, and then describing it as what He has approved for them, there is a winning of their hearts, an increase of encouragement to it, and a great favour of confirmation upon it.

﴿and He will surely change them﴾ with the doubled consonant (*tashdid*). It is also read with the single consonant (*takhfif*), from the verb *ibdal* (to exchange). ﴿after their fear﴾, that is, fear of enemies, ﴿to security﴾. For the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were in fear before the Hijrah for ten years, indeed more, and then they emigrated to Medina. They would be in arms in the morning and likewise in the evening. Until one man of them said: "There will not come upon us a day in which we are secure." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You will not wait except a little while until one of you sits in the great assembly, reclining with his legs drawn up, having no weapon with him." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse, fulfilled His promise, and gave them mastery over the Arabian Peninsula, opened for them the lands of East and West, and they came to a state in which everyone other than them feared them. In this there is, by the foretelling of the unseen as it would be before it occurred, a proof of the truth of prophethood that is not hidden. It has also been said: the intended meaning is fear of punishment and security from it in the Hereafter.

﴿They worship Me﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the first relative pronoun, indicating that the promise is restricted to persistence in monotheism. Or it is a resumptive sentence explaining the cause that necessitates the succession and what is arranged with it in the course of the promise.

﴿not associating anything with Me﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the waw (of the plural), meaning: they worship Me without associating anything with Me in worship.

﴿But whoever disbelieves﴾, that is, is characterised by disbelief, by being firm and persisting in it, and not being affected by what has passed of warning and encouragement. For persistence in it after witnessing the proofs of monotheism is disbelief, a new disbelief added to the original one. It has also been said: he disbelieved after faith; it has also been said: he disbelieved this great blessing. The first is more fitting to the context.

﴿after that﴾, that is, after that noble promise, with what has been detailed of the lofty aims which make it necessary to give utmost attention to attaining them and to striving nobly to possess them.

﴿those are﴾ the remote ones from the truth, wandering in the bewilderment of error and misguidance, ﴿the defiantly disobedient﴾, those who are perfect in transgression and in going beyond the limits of disbelief and insolence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 56:

﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to an implied element (muqaddar) that the discourse extends over and that the arrangement (niẓām) calls for. For His, exalted is He, address to those commanded to obedience is by way of warning (tarhīb) against turning away, through His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if they turn away…﴾ etc., and His encouragement (targhīb) of them to obedience through His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾ etc.; His promise to them of faith and righteous deeds through what has been detailed of the succession (istikhlaf) and what follows it of the desired rewards promised; and His threat concerning disbelief. This necessitates the command to faith and righteous deeds and the prohibition of disbelief. So it is as if it were said: "Then believe, do righteous deeds, and establish [prayer]," or "Then do not disbelieve, and establish [prayer]." Its conjunction to "Obey Allah" is not befitting the eloquence (jazālah) of the noble arrangement.

﴿And obey the Messenger﴾: Allah, glory be to Him and exalted is He, commanded them directly with what He commanded them through the mediation of the Messenger (ﷺ) of obedience to him, which is in reality obedience to Him, exalted is He, as an emphasis (taʾkīd) of the previous command and a confirmation (taqrīr) of its content. This is on the basis that what is meant by "that which is obeyed" in it is all the legal rulings (aḥkām sharʿiyyah) that comprise the praiseworthy ethical norms (ādāb al-marḍiyyah) as well; that is: "And obey him in everything he commands you and forbids you." Or [it is] a completion (takmīl) of what precedes it of the two specific commands relating to prayer and zakah, on the basis that what is meant by what is mentioned is what is other than them of the laws; that is: "And obey him in all that he commands you," etc.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may be shown mercy﴾ is connected, according to the first view, to the last command, which encompasses all the commands, and according to the second view, to the three commands; that is: do what has been mentioned of establishing, giving and obeying, hoping that you will be shown mercy.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 57:

﴿Do not suppose that those who disbelieve﴾ When He (Exalted is He) had explained the condition of those who obeyed him (ﷺ), and alluded to their success with absolute mercy, which entails the happiness of both abodes, this was followed by an explanation of the condition of those who disobeyed him (ﷺ), and the outcome of their affair in this world and the Hereafter, after explaining how far they had gone in wickedness, to complete the matter of encouragement and warning. The address is either to every person who is fit for it, whoever he may be, or to the Messenger (ﷺ), following the pattern of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ and its like, to make known that the supposition mentioned is of such ugliness and reprehensibility that one who cannot possibly commit it is forbidden from it, so how about one for whom it is possible?

The place of the relative pronoun is in the accusative, as it is the first object of "to suppose" (ḥusbān), and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿incapable﴾ is the second of them. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿in the earth﴾ is an adverbial complement of "incapable", but not to indicate that the incapacity being negated is in it and not in anything else, for that does not need explaining. Rather, it is to indicate that the absence of incapacity extends to all its parts. That is: do not suppose them to be incapable of [escaping] Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from their apprehension and destruction in any region of the earth, however vast it is, even if they flee from it every way of escape.

It has also been read: "Let not ... suppose" (lā yaḥsabanna) with the yā' of the third person, the subject being "everyone", and the meaning is as mentioned: that is, let no one suppose the disbelievers to be incapable of Him, glorified is He, in the earth. Or the subject is the relative pronoun, and the first object is omitted because it refers to themselves, as if it were said: Do not suppose that the disbelievers themselves are incapable in the earth. As for making "incapable" the first object and "in the earth" the second object, it is far from agreeing with what the context requires, since the thrust of the benefit lies in the second object, and there is no benefit in stating that the incapable are in the earth, a matter already discussed in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I am making in the earth a successor﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ is coordinated with the prohibitive clause, by interpreting it as a declarative clause, because the purpose of the prohibition against supposing is to establish the negation of that supposition, as if it were said: "Those who disbelieved are not incapable, and their refuge is ..." etc. Or it is coordinated with an implied clause which serves as a reason for the prohibition, as if it were said: "Do not suppose that those who disbelieve are incapable in the earth, for they are overtaken, and their refuge is," etc. It has been said that the implied clause is: "Rather, they are subdued", so reflect.

﴿And wretched is the destination﴾ is an answer to an implied oath, and the object of the dispraise is omitted, that is: "By Allah, wretched is the destination, it," i.e., the Fire. The sentence is a parenthetical concluding clause confirming what precedes it. In presenting the Fire under the description of being their refuge and destination immediately after negating their escape by fleeing in every way of the earth, there is an eloquence beyond which there is no further limit. So by God, how excellent is the composition of the Revelation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 58:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ This is a return to explaining the completion of the previously mentioned rulings, after preparing the ground with what necessitates compliance with the commands and prohibitions contained in them and in the following rulings, such as the illustrations, encouragement and warning, promise and threat. The address is either to men specifically, with women included in the ruling by indication of the text (dalalat al-nass), or to both groups together by way of predominance (taghlib).

It is narrated that a boy belonging to Asma' bint Abi Murthad entered upon her at a time she disliked, and so this was revealed. It is also said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Mudlij ibn 'Amr al-Ansari, who was a boy, at midday to summon 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. He entered upon him while he was asleep, his garment having become uncovered from him. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'I wish that Allah, Exalted, had forbidden our fathers, our sons and our servants from entering upon us at these hours except with permission.' Then he set off with him to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and found that this verse had been revealed to him."

﴿That those whom your right hands possess﴾ of the slaves and the female slaves, ﴿and those among you who have not reached puberty﴾ i.e., the children who have not attained the known level of puberty. Its expression by "puberty" (hulm) is because it is its most evident sign among you, i.e., among the free.

﴿three times﴾ i.e., three times in the day and night. The expression of them as "times" indicates that the basis of the obligation of seeking permission is the coincidence of those times with the passage of those seeking permission upon those addressed, not the times themselves.

﴿Before the prayer of dawn﴾ because it is evident that it is the time of rising from beds, casting off sleeping garments and putting on waking garments. Its position is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "three times," or in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., one of them is "before..." and so on.

﴿and when you put off your clothes﴾ i.e., your clothes which you wear in the day and take off for the sake of the midday rest (qailulah). His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿at midday﴾, which is the intense heat at the middle of the day, is an explanation of the time, and an explicit statement of the basis of the matter, I mean the putting off of clothes, at this time rather than the first and last (of the day), because stripping of clothes in it is for the sake of the midday rest, owing to its brevity, as the attachment of "time" to a transient, passing act indicates. Its occurrence in the day, which is the locus of frequent coming and going and the place of the manifestation of conditions and the emergence of affairs, is not of the same certainty and regularity as what occurs in the two mentioned times, for the certainty and regularity of stripping in those two is a known matter that does not need to be stated explicitly.

﴿and after the prayer of 'Isha'﴾ since it is evidently the time of stripping of clothing and wrapping oneself in a blanket. The intended meaning of the "before" and "after" mentioned is not their absolute senses, which would be realized in the extended period lying between the two prayers, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed you were before it among the unaware﴾ and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿after Satan had sown discord between me and my brothers﴾, but rather what occurs at the two extremities of that extended period, adjoining the two mentioned prayers by ordinary contiguity.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿three times of nakedness (awrat)﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿for you﴾ is connected to an omitted element which is an attribute of "three times of nakedness," i.e., existing for you. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) given to explain the reason for the obligation of seeking permission, i.e., these are three times in which concealment ordinarily breaks down. ʿAwrah in origin means a defect; it has become predominantly used for a defect in what is important to protect and cared to conceal, and it was applied to the times containing these as an intensification, as if they were the very nakedness itself. It is also read "three times of nakedness" in the accusative as a substitute for "three times."

﴿There is no blame upon you or upon them﴾ i.e., upon the slaves and children there is no sin (junah), i.e., no sin in entering without permission, because of the absence of what would necessitate it, namely contravening the command and gaining sight of nakedness.

﴿after them﴾ i.e., after each one of those three times of nakedness, which are the times intervening between every two of them. Its presentation under the heading of "after" although each of these times is before one of the nakednesses, just as it is after another of them, is to fulfil the right of obligation and dispensation, which is an expression for lifting it, since dispensation is only conceived in an act that occurs after the time of the act obligated. The sentence, on both readings, is a resumptive clause given to affirm what precedes it by direct and reverse statement. It has been permitted on the first reading that it be in the nominative position as another attribute of "three times of nakedness." As for the second reading, it is purely a resumptive clause, for if it were made an attribute of "three times of nakedness" while "three times" is a substitute, the meaning would be: "Let these seek your permission in three times of nakedness; there is no sin in abandoning seeking permission after them," and since the absence of sin in that case is something the hearer would not know except through this statement, it could not be presented in the form of an attribute. By contrast, with the nominative reading, the absence of sin is known from the beginning of the sentence.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿They go about among you﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining the excuse that permits abandoning seeking permission, namely constant mutual contact and frequent entry. In it is evidence for the causation of rulings, and likewise in the distinction between the three times and others by their being "nakedness."

﴿some of you upon others﴾ i.e., some of you circulate upon others in much circulation, or some of you goes about to others.

﴿Thus﴾ is a reference to the verbal noun of the verb that follows it, and what it contains of the sense of distance, as has been repeated many times, is for the magnification of the status of what is referred to and to indicate the distance of its rank and its being, in clarity, like what is pointed to sensibly, i.e., like that clarification.

﴿Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾ which indicate the rulings, i.e., He sends them down clear, with evident indications of them, not that He, exalted, clarifies them after they were not so. The particle "kaf" is superfluous (muqhimah), and its detailed treatment has passed in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We have made you a justly balanced nation﴾. "For you" is connected to "makes clear," and its placement before the explicit object is, as has been repeated many times, for the concern with what is placed first and the arousing of anticipation for what is placed later. It has been said that it makes clear the causes (ʿilal) of the rulings, but this is not evident, and moreover it leads to restricting the verses to what has been mentioned here.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ intensively in knowledge of all knowables, so He knows your conditions ﴿All-Wise﴾ in all His acts, so He legislates for you what contains the welfare of your affairs in this life and the hereafter.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 59:

﴿And when the children among you reach puberty (al-hulm), let them ask permission﴾ as those before them asked permission. This is connected to what was explained just before: the ruling concerning children, that there is no blame upon them for not seeking permission outside the three times. It is followed by an explanation of their condition after puberty, to repel what might be imagined, namely that they, although they are strangers (ajanib), are not like other strangers because of their habit of entering (the houses). That is: when the free children who are strangers reach puberty, ﴿let them ask permission﴾ whenever they wish to enter upon you.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿as those before them asked permission﴾: it is in the place of the accusative, as an adjective (na't) of a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing the preceding verb. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) refers to those to whom it was said: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought familiarity...﴾, to the end of the verse. He described them as being "before these" with respect to their being mentioned before them, not with respect to their reaching puberty before them, as some have said. This is because the purpose of the comparison is to explain the manner of these people's asking permission and to clarify it further, and this can only be achieved by comparing it to the asking permission of those well known to the listener. There is no doubt that their reaching puberty before these others is something that does not occur to anyone's mind, even if it is so in reality. What is known and familiar is their being mentioned before them. That is: ﴿let them ask permission﴾ in a manner like the asking permission of those mentioned before them, by asking permission at all times, and by returning if they are told "Return," as has been detailed earlier.

﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you His verses, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ The discussion of this is like that which preceded it; the repetition is for emphasis and for intensifying the command to ask permission. The attribution of the verses to the Divine Name (damir al-jalalah) is to honor them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 60:

﴿And as for women past child-bearing (al-qawa'id min al-nisa')﴾, that is: the old women who have ceased from menstruation and childbearing, ﴿who have no hope of marriage﴾, that is: who do not desire it because of their advanced age, ﴿there is no blame upon them if they put aside their outer garments﴾, that is: the outer garments such as the jilbab (a loose outer cloak) and the like. The fa' (fa'-"then") here is because the lam in al-qawa'id carries the meaning of alladhi/allati (who), or because it is a descriptive qualification by it.

﴿without displaying adornment (ghayra mutabarrijat bi-zinah)﴾, that is: not showing off any adornment of the kind they were commanded to conceal in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and not to reveal their adornment﴾. The root of tabarruj (display) is: the affectation of showing what is hidden, from the saying of them: "a ship that is barij", meaning one with no covering over it. And al-baraj is: the breadth of the eye such that its whiteness surrounds all of its blackness, except that it was specialized to the woman uncovering her adornment and her charms for men.

﴿But that they refrain (wa-an yasta'fifna)﴾ by not putting them aside ﴿is better for them﴾ than putting them aside, because it is further from suspicion.

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing (sami')﴾, an intensive form, hearing all that is heard, so He hears what passes between them and the men of conversation ﴿All-Knowing (alim)﴾, so He knows their intentions. And in this there is a warning that is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 61:

﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves﴾. These groups used to avoid eating with the healthy, out of fear that the healthy would find them repulsive and out of fear of being harmed by their actions and conditions. The blind man's hand may often reach for what his companion's eye has reached, without his noticing it. The lame man may spread out in his seat and take more than his share of space, thereby crowding his companion. (p-196) The sick man is never free of some condition that harms his companion. It was also said: they used to enter upon a man seeking knowledge, and if he did not have anything to feed them, he would take them to the houses of their fathers and mothers, or to some of those whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, named in the noble verse. They would avoid this and say: "He has taken us to the house of someone else, and perhaps its people dislike that." Likewise, they used to avoid eating from the property of those who, when they went out to fight, left these people in their houses, handed them the keys, and gave them permission to eat from what was in them, for fear that their permission was not given with full consent. Others besides these groups also avoided eating in the houses of other people. So it was said to them: there is no blame upon the aforementioned groups, ﴿nor upon yourselves﴾, meaning: there is no blame upon you or upon those among the believers who are similar to you in circumstances, ﴿to eat﴾, meaning: that you eat, while they eat with you. The generalization of the address to the aforementioned groups also is rejected by what precedes and follows it, since the address in both of them is definitely to other than those groups.

﴿From your houses﴾, meaning: the houses in which your wives and dependents are, and this includes the houses of your children, because their house is like his, due to his saying (ﷺ): "You and your wealth belong to your father," and his saying (ﷺ): "Indeed the best of a man's earnings is from his own work, and indeed his child is part of his earnings."

﴿Or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers﴾. It is recited with a kasra on the hamza and the mim, and with a kasra on the first and a fatha on the second (a canonical reading, qira'a, of the word for "houses" and its vowels).

﴿Or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts, or what you hold the keys to﴾, meaning: from the houses over which you have the right of disposal by the permission of their owners, in the manner explained earlier. It was also said: these are the houses of slaves. The word for "keys" (maftah) is the plural of miftah (key), and the plural of miftah is maftih. It is also recited as "miftahahu" (its key, singular).

﴿Or your friend﴾, meaning: or the houses of your friend, even if there is no lineal kinship between you and them, for they are more pleased with and more delighted by such familiarity than many relatives are. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) that a friend is greater than parents, since when the people of Hell cried out for help, they did not call upon fathers and mothers, but said: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor any close friend﴾. The word "friend" (sadiq) applies to the singular and plural, like khalit and qatin and their likes. This applies when the consent of the owner of the house is known, either by explicit permission or by a clear indication. For this reason these people were singled out for mention, because they habitually relax with one another.

His Exalted saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you in eating together or separately﴾ is a resumptive statement, brought to explain another ruling of the same kind as what was explained before, since a group of believers, such as the Banu Layth ibn 'Amr of Kinana, used to avoid eating their food alone. A man among them would not eat and would remain the whole day until he found a guest to eat with him. If he did not find anyone to eat with him, he would not eat anything. Sometimes a man would sit with food before him and not take any of it from morning until evening. Sometimes he had camels that were milk-giving, yet he would not drink their milk until he found someone to drink with him. When evening came and he had found no one, he would eat. It was also said: a wealthy one among them would enter upon a poor relative or a poor person to whom he gave charity, and invite him to his food, and the poor person would say: "I avoid eating with you, since I am wealthy and you are poor." It was also said: some of the Ansar would not eat, when a guest arrived, except together with their guest, so they were given leave to eat however they wished. It was also said: when they gathered to eat a meal, they would set aside a portion of food for the blind and those like him, in a fixed amount, so Allah, Exalted, made clear that this was not obligatory.

His Exalted saying: "jami'an" (together) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the subject of "ta'kulu" (you eat). "Ashtatan" (separately) is conjoined to it and falls under its ruling. It is the plural of "shatt," used as an adjective, like "haqq," as in one says: "amr shatt," meaning: a scattered matter. Or it is, originally, a verbal noun (masdar) described by it for emphasis, meaning: there is no blame upon you in eating gathered together or scattered apart.

﴿So when you enter﴾: this begins an explanation of the etiquettes that must be observed when one undertakes what has been permitted, immediately after the explanation of the permission regarding it.

﴿Houses﴾, meaning: from the aforementioned houses (p-197). ﴿Then greet one another﴾, meaning: greet those who live in them, who are like yourselves, because of the religious and lineal kinship between you and them, which necessitates this.

﴿A greeting from Allah﴾, meaning: established by His command and legislated from Him. It is also permissible for it to be a complement of "greeting," since it is a request for life, which is from Him, Exalted. Its accusative status is as a verbal noun (masdar), because it has the meaning of "greeting."

﴿Blessed﴾, meaning: bringing with it increase of goodness and reward, and their continuance.

﴿Good﴾, meaning: that by it the soul of the listener is made content. It is reported from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whenever you meet anyone of my community, greet him, and your life will be lengthened. When you enter your house, greet its people, and the good of your house will increase. Pray the Duha prayer, for it is the prayer of the righteous who turn back in repentance."

﴿Thus does Allah make the signs clear to you﴾: a repetition to confirm the rulings that are concluded with it and to magnify them. ﴿So that you may understand﴾, meaning: what is in their contents of laws and rulings, and that you may act in accordance with what they require, and thereby attain the happiness of both abodes. In the grounding of this clarification upon this supreme purpose, after concluding the first (verses) with what makes them necessary, of eloquence and grandeur, there is what is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 62:

﴿Indeed, the believers are those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), placed at the end of the preceding rulings, to confirm them, to emphasize the obligation of observing them, and to complete them by clarifying another part of the same kind. The mention of belief in Allah and His Messenger within the relative clause (silah) of the relative pronoun that serves as the predicate of the subject is, together with its definite implication of it, a confirmation of what precedes it, a preparation for what follows, and an indication that it deserves to be made a companion of belief in both of them, arranged in the same string. So the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when they are with him upon a matter of common concern﴾ and so on, are conjoined to "believed" (amanu) and are included with it in the scope of the relative clause. That is: indeed, the perfect in faith are those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger from the depths of their hearts and obeyed both of them in all the rulings, among which are those detailed earlier concerning their general affairs that occur constantly and their circumstances that occur by chance, such as when they are with him ﷺ upon an important matter requiring their gathering concerning it, such as Friday prayer, the festivals, wars, and other matters calling for the gathering of people of opinion and experience. The description of the matter as "gathering" (jami') is for emphasis. It was also read: "upon a matter that is all-encompassing" (amrin jami').

﴿Have not gone away﴾ That is: from the assembly, although that matter is one that does not necessarily require their presence, as in the establishment of Friday prayer and encountering the enemy, but rather permits absence from it.

﴿Until they have sought his permission﴾ ﷺ to depart. Not that seeking permission itself is the limit for not departing; rather the limit is the permission that depends on his opinion, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Mention is restricted to it because it is what is completed on their part, and it is what is considered in the perfection of faith, not the permission itself nor the departure that results from it. Its being taken into account in this matter is because it is like a proof of its soundness and a distinguisher of the sincere person in it from the hypocrite, for the hypocrite's habit is to slip away to flee. And to magnify the sin of departing without his permission ﷺ, and to draw attention to this, He follows it with the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who seek your permission, they are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. So He judges that those who seek permission are the believers in Allah and His Messenger, just as He ruled at the beginning that the perfect in faith are those who combine belief in both of them with seeking permission. In "those" (ulaika) there is an exaltation of the status of those who seek permission that is not hidden.

﴿So when they seek your permission﴾ is an explanation of what is his function ﷺ in this matter, following the explanation of what is the function of the believers, and that permission at the time of seeking it is not a binding command but is entrusted to his opinion ﷺ. The fa' (so) is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes it, that is: after it has been established that the perfect in faith are those who seek permission, then when they seek your permission ﴿for some of their affairs﴾ that is: for some of their important matters and pressing business, ﴿grant permission to whomever you wish of them﴾ because of the wisdom and benefit you know in that, ﴿and ask Allah's forgiveness for them﴾, for seeking permission, even if it is for a strong excuse, is not free from a trace of preferring the affair of this world over the affair of the Hereafter.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ exceedingly in forgiving the lapses of servants ﴿Merciful﴾ exceedingly in bestowing the effects of mercy upon them. The sentence is a reason for the forgiveness promised within the command to seek forgiveness for them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 63:

﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among yourselves like the calling of some of you to others.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that confirms the content of what precedes it. The shift (iltifat) to the third person is to highlight the greater importance of his status. That is: do not make his ﷺ call to you, whether in belief or in action upon it, like your calling to one another. ﴿Like the calling of some of you to others﴾ means: do not equate his ﷺ calling you with your calling one another in any state or any matter, among which is being lax about it and leaving his ﷺ assembly without seeking permission, for that is among the forbidden acts. It has also been said: do not make his ﷺ calling upon his Lord like the calling of your young to your elder, whom he answers once and rejects another time, for his supplication is answered and there is no turning it back with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The statement, in that case, confirms what precedes it, either in that His answering his ﷺ supplication necessitates that they obey his commands, peace and blessings be upon him, and follow him in coming and going in the most complete obligation; or in that it necessitates refraining from provoking his ﷺ anger, which leads to what would bring about their destruction through his ﷺ supplication against them. As for what has been said, that the meaning is: do not make his ﷺ calling like your calling one another by name, raising the voice, and calling from behind the apartments, but rather by his exalted title, such as "O Messenger of Allah" or "O Prophet of Allah", with the utmost reverence, glorification, humility and lowering of the voice, it does not fit the context. For His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah already knows those of you who slip away﴾ and so on, is a warning to those who oppose his command ﷺ regarding what was mentioned earlier, so placing what is mentioned between them is without justification. Tasallul (slipping away) is leaving the house gradually and secretly, and "qad" is for emphasis of certainty, just as rubba comes for multiplicity, as explained at the beginning of Surat al-Hijr. That is: Allah knows those who leave the gathering little by little, in secret.

﴿Liwadhan﴾ means: concealing themselves, by one hiding behind another until he leaves, or by clinging to one who leaves with permission, so as to show that he is one of his followers. It has been read with a fatha on the lam, and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "yatasallaluna", meaning: concealing themselves; or as an emphatic infinitive (masdar) for an implied verb which is in reality the state, meaning: they cling to one another (yalludhuna liwadhan). The fa' in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware﴾ is for the arrangement of beware, or of the command to beware, upon what precedes it, namely His knowledge, Exalted is He, of their conditions, for that is definitely something that necessitates beware. That is: they oppose his command by abandoning its requirement and go in a manner contrary to his manner. "'An" is either because it includes the meaning of turning away, or it is taken to mean: they turn away from his command, excluding the believers; one who opposes him regarding the command, when he turns away from it, excluding him. The object is omitted because the intent is to explain the one who opposes and the one opposed. The pronoun refers to Allah, Exalted, because He is the actual commander, or to the Messenger ﷺ because he is the one intended by the mention.

﴿Lest a trial befall them﴾ means: a calamity in this world; ﴿or a painful punishment befall them﴾ means: in the Hereafter. The word "aw" (or) here denotes preventing the absence of both, not preventing their combination, and the verb is repeated explicitly (p-199) for emphasis on the threat and warning. It has been used as evidence that the command denotes obligation, for the ordering of the two punishments upon opposing it, as the warning against befalling by them expresses, necessitates the obligation to comply with it absolutely.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 24, verse 64:

﴿Surely to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ of existing things in their entirety, in creation, dominion and disposal, in bringing into being and annihilating, in beginning and returning.

﴿He knows your condition﴾ O you who are accountable, of the states and circumstances, among which are agreement and opposition, sincerity and hypocrisy.

﴿And the Day they are returned to Him﴾ is conjoined with "your condition" — that is, He knows the Day on which the hypocrites who oppose the command are returned to Him, Exalted is He, for recompense and punishment. The linking of His knowledge to the Day of their return does not indicate an increase in the confirmation of His knowledge of that, and it is the utmost affirmation of it, since knowledge of the time of an event's occurrence necessarily entails acting upon its occurrence in the most emphatic and forceful manner. In it there is an indication that His knowledge of the very fact of their return is so evident that it needs no explanation, with certainty. It is also permissible that the address is specifically to the hypocrites, in the manner of the shift (iltifat) in address. It has been read: "yarji'un" with the active voice (yarji'una).

﴿Then He will inform them of what they did﴾ of the evil deeds, among which is opposition to the command, so there will follow from it what befits it of rebuke and recompense. The reason for expressing recompense by "informing" has already been explained in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your rebellion is only against yourselves...﴾ the verse.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ nothing escapes your Lord, of an atom's weight on the earth or in the heaven.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Whoever recites Surah al-Nur will be given the reward of ten good deeds for every believing man and believing woman, past and future.﴾ And Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows best.
